arc:
The series follows Dorothy's repeated crossings between Kansas and the Land of Oz, and the widening circle of companions she draws into Oz's defense along the way. The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion, whose quests for a brain, a heart, and courage are resolved in the first tome, remain bound to Oz afterward — the Scarecrow left to rule the Emerald City in the Wizard's place, the Tin Woodman established as Emperor of the Winkies — and are joined across later tomes by other travelers such as Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, Zeb, Jim, and Eureka, who are likewise drawn into Oz's affairs and, in several cases, into Ozma's court.

Running through the tomes is the question of who rightfully governs Oz. The Wizard, revealed to be a humbug, departs by balloon and leaves the Scarecrow to rule; that rule is contested when General Jinjur leads an army of girls to seize the Emerald City, and the crisis is only resolved when Old Mombi is forced to confess that the boy Tip is in fact the transformed Princess Ozma, the true heir hidden since infancy, who is then crowned. Ozma's reign is subsequently defended both from within, against Jinjur's revolt, and from without, against the Nome King, who threatens the Queen of Ev's family in one tome and later invades the Emerald City itself in another, each time repelled through the Scarecrow's and Ozma's stratagems and through the power of magical instruments — the Golden Cap, and above all the Magic Belt taken from the Nome King — that pass between rulers and protectors of Oz.

Dorothy's own place in this world is never settled for good: she is carried home to Kansas at the end of her first adventure, sent instead to convalesce with Uncle Henry in Australia after a later one, returned to Kansas again following an earthquake that drops her into Oz's underground, and brought home once more from Ozma's birthday celebrations, always by way of the Magic Belt or its like. Each return underscores travel between Kansas and Oz, and the assembling of new friends into Ozma's circle, as the rhythm that carries the series from its first tome to its last.

page.title: Dorothy
page.content:
## Biography

Dorothy is a girl traveling the road of yellow brick toward the Emerald City in the company of the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion, together with her dog Toto. She undertakes the journey in hope of reaching the Great Oz, telling her companions that reaching the Emerald City is necessary if she is ever to get back to Kansas, where her Aunt Em and Uncle Henry live.

Passing through a dense forest still covered by the yellow brick road, Dorothy walks close beside Toto, who senses danger the others cannot perceive. When a Lion leaps from the trees and threatens to bite Toto, Dorothy rushes forward without regard for her own safety and strikes the Lion across the nose, rebuking him for menacing "a poor little dog."

During the journey, Dorothy shares what remains of her bread with Toto and later builds a fire to warm the camp for the night; the Scarecrow gathers nuts for her basket and covers her with dry leaves so that she sleeps warmly until morning. Crossing a river afterward on a raft built by the Tin Woodman, she sits at its center holding Toto while the Scarecrow and the Woodman use long poles to steady and push the raft through the water.

In a later stretch of the journey, Dorothy awakens from a long sleep to find herself lying in the grass surrounded by thousands of field mice, and is introduced to their Queen by the Scarecrow. She later thanks the mice for having saved the Cowardly Lion, whom she has grown fond of.

Continuing on the road of yellow brick, Dorothy and her companions eventually reach a country of green fields and arrive at the Emerald City, where the streets are lined with green marble houses studded with emeralds and the inhabitants dress entirely in green. There, the Guardian of the Gates tells her there is no road leading to the Wicked Witch of the West. After leaving the palace and turning west, Dorothy notices that her silk dress, until then green, has turned white, as has the ribbon around Toto's neck.

## Narrative role

Dorothy lives with Uncle Henry and Aunt Em in a small house on the gray Kansas prairies, where Toto, her small black dog, is the one lively, cheerful presence in her life. When a storm threatens, Aunt Em orders Dorothy to the storm cellar and climbs down first while Dorothy searches for Toto.

Later, further along her journey, Dorothy and her companions continue walking through thick, overgrown woods, still following the road of yellow brick. This leads her to Oz, whom she first meets as a giant disembodied Head; Oz agrees to send her home only if she kills the Wicked Witch of the West.

Sent to carry out this task, Dorothy is tricked by the Witch into losing one Silver Shoe, but when Dorothy angrily throws water on her, the Witch melts away and dies, ending her tyranny. Dorothy then declares the Winkies free from the years of cruel servitude they suffered under the Witch. The Winkies give her parting gifts, she takes the Golden Cap from the Witch's cupboard, and the group sets off for the Emerald City to claim Oz's promises. Along the way, Dorothy frees the Cowardly Lion from his prison after learning that the Wicked Witch has melted, and together with the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Lion, she becomes lost in fields of buttercups and daisies while trying to walk back to the Emerald City.

Back at the palace, Oz promises to give brains, courage, and a heart the next day, and asks for time to find a way to send Dorothy back to Kansas; left alone, he privately admits to himself that he is a humbug and worries he has no idea how to do so. On the fourth day, Oz summons Dorothy and proposes crossing the desert by balloon, since he cannot make a cyclone. The Tin Woodman, the Scarecrow, and the Lion praise Oz for granting their wishes, while Dorothy privately forgives him for not keeping his promise to her.

Glinda agrees to receive Dorothy and her companions at once. Dorothy bids a tearful farewell to her companions, clicks her heels together, and is instantly whirled back to the Kansas prairie, though the Silver Shoes are lost during the flight; Glinda had agreed to help her but asked for the Golden Cap in exchange, which Dorothy willingly gave up. Once home, Toto has returned with Dorothy.

## Personality

Dorothy shows protective courage toward her companion Toto: when the Cowardly Lion opens his mouth to bite the dog, she rushes forward heedless of danger and slaps the Lion's nose, crying, "Don't you dare to bite Toto! You ought to be ashamed of yourself, a big beast like you, to bite a poor little dog!" Her indignation targets the unfairness of a large beast threatening a small creature.

She is also attentive and appreciative toward those who help her. When the Scarecrow fills her basket with nuts despite his awkward, straw-stuffed hands, she finds it "very kind and thoughtful," laughing at his clumsiness without mockery. Toward the Queen of the Field Mice and the mice who pull the Cowardly Lion from the poppy field, she responds with warm gratitude, having "grown so fond of the big Lion she was glad he had been rescued."

Dorothy is loyal to her traveling companions, describing the Lion to a wary farmhouse woman as "my friend and comrade" who "would not hurt you for the world." Alongside this loyalty runs a steady homesickness: she states plainly, "I should never get back to Kansas," a concern that recurs together with her determination to reach the Emerald City.

## Appearance

Dorothy wears a silk dress given to her within the palace of the Emerald City. While she remains inside the city, the dress appears green, like everything around her there. After leaving the city and turning west, she finds, to her surprise, that the dress is no longer green but pure white — as is the ribbon around Toto's neck, which had also lost its green color.

## Relationships

**[[Scarecrow]]** — the pair's exchanges suggest a close friendship: he fills Dorothy's basket with nuts so she would not go hungry, and each night comes near only to cover her with dry leaves, keeping her snug and warm while she sleeps.

**[[Cowardly Lion]]** — the bond suggests genuine affection: Dorothy is said to have "grown so fond of the big Lion" that she is glad when the field mice save him from the poison of the poppy field, and she later assures a wary farmwife that "the Lion is my friend and comrade" who "would not hurt you for the world."

**[[Tin Woodman]]** — appears to be a trusted travelling companion: he chops wood to build their campfire and constructs the raft meant to carry the group toward the Emerald City, providing for Dorothy through the hardest stretches of the journey.

**[[Toto]]** — suggests a deep, protective attachment: hearing the dog threatened, Dorothy rushes forward heedless of danger and strikes the Lion's nose, crying, "Don't you dare to bite Toto! You ought to be ashamed of yourself, a big beast like you, to bite a poor little dog!"

**[[Aunt Em]]** — seems to indicate a close family tie: Dorothy asks to be sent back to Kansas "where my Aunt Em and Uncle Henry are," and worries that "Aunt Em will be dreadfully worried over my being away so long."

## Trivia

- The silk dress given to Dorothy in the Emerald City was green, but the moment she and her companions passed beyond the city's borders, the dress turned pure white — the ribbon around Toto's neck lost its green color at the same time and turned white as well.
- Upon waking the morning after camping in the forest, she breakfasted "like a princess" on peaches and plums gathered from trees beside a river.
- When she and her companions arrived at the Palace of Oz, she was given a green room and new clothes by a green-haired attendant while her friends rested separately.
- When introduced to the Queen of the Field Mice by the Scarecrow, Dorothy nodded gravely as the Queen curtsied to her, and the two became friendly afterward.

page.title: Dorothy
page.content:
## Biography

Dorothy is a girl who came to the Land of Oz from Kansas, a place in the big, outside World. Alongside the Tin Woodman, she helped destroy the Wicked Witch of the West, an act for which the grateful Winkies made the Tin Woodman their ruler. The Scarecrow recalls once saving her from the Stinging Bees of the Wicked Witch of the West. Scenes from her past adventures with the Tin Woodman, the Cowardly Lion, and the Scarecrow are engraved upon a silver oil-can kept in the Tin Woodman's palace. She had also spoken to others of the terrible outside world lying beyond the sandy deserts that surround the Land of Oz.

## Relationships

**[[The Scarecrow]]** — ally. The Scarecrow, described as one of Dorothy's friends, is said to have once saved her from the Stinging Bees of the Wicked Witch of the West, suggesting a protective bond between them.

**[[Glinda the Good]]** — ally. An inferred connection to Glinda the Good hints at a possible bond, though its exact nature remains uncertain.

**[[Nick Chopper]]** — ally. Nick Chopper, the Tin Woodman, is said to have helped Dorothy destroy the Wicked Witch of the West, suggesting an allied history between them.

**[[Wizard of Oz]]** — enemy. Some accounts suggest an antagonistic history between Dorothy and the Wizard of Oz.

page.title: DOROTHY
page.content:
## Biography

Dorothy, also known as Kansas, travels as part of Ozma's court and keeps a hen named Billina as her pet, carrying her closely and defending her without hesitation. When the Hungry Tiger admits Billina's appearance "makes my mouth water," Dorothy answers at once, "Billina is my friend, and you mustn't ever eat her under any circ'mstances," and she reacts with alarm, crying out "WHY, BILLINA! HAVE YOU BEEN FIGHTING?" upon seeing the hen roughed up.

She is present when Billina reveals that the Prince had unknowingly carried the Tin Woodman, trapped, inside his pocket after taking his enchanted whistle. Dorothy questions Billina directly — "What do you mean?" — as the hen explains, and when Billina sounds the whistle to free him, the Tin Woodman reappears and greets both Dorothy and the Prince by name, bowing to them.

At the royal court of Ev, Dorothy is counted among those "splendidly entertained" by the Queen mother alongside Ozma, Tiktok, and Billina, following the resolution of the royal family's troubles and the crowning of Evardo as King of Ev. Afterward, in the Emerald City, Dorothy decides to accept Ozma's invitation to return with her to the Land of Oz.

Within the palace of Ev, Dorothy carries her pet hen into the drawing-room, where a chair is kept vacant for her among the gathered company that includes Ozma, Tiktok, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and Princess Langwidere — a seat reserved for her within this circle.

## Narrative role

Dorothy, also known as Kansas, joins an expedition led by Ozma, alongside the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, Tiktok, Billina, the Cowardly Lion, and the army of Oz, marching to free the [[Queen of Ev]] and her ten children from the Nome King. When given the chance to guess among the Nome King's ornaments, Dorothy succeeds in freeing Prince Evring, the youngest son of the Queen of Ev. When Nome warriors attack the group, the Scarecrow throws Billina's poisonous eggs at the King, and in the resulting confusion Dorothy steals his magic belt, gaining power over its enchantments.

Afterward, Dorothy bids farewell to her friends in Oz, including Billina, who chooses to stay behind, and is transported to Uncle Henry in Australia, where she comforts him as he recovers.

Glinda the Good advises that the magic belt only works within fairy countries, so Dorothy gives the belt to Ozma, who agrees to bring her back to Oz whenever she signals on a Saturday.

Ozma's party, including Dorothy, Tiktok, and Billina, crosses the desert on the magic carpet and travels to the Emerald City, meeting Jinjur, now a contented farm wife, along the way.

Using Ozma's magic picture, Dorothy checks on Aunt Em, who is well and content, and on Uncle Henry, who is in Australia, sad and unwell, and decides she must return to him.

## Personality

Dorothy shows quick, firm loyalty toward Billina, the hen she keeps close as a companion: when the Hungry Tiger eyes Billina with open appetite, Dorothy answers "hastily" that Billina is her friend and "mustn't ever eat her under any circ'mstances," a decisive defense offered the instant the threat appears. That same protectiveness surfaces as alarm when she finds Billina looking disheveled, crying out "WHY, BILLINA! HAVE YOU BEEN FIGHTING?" — a reflexive concern for a companion's welfare before any explanation is given.

Dorothy also proves inquisitive when a situation puzzles her. On hearing Billina's cryptic remark that explains why the Tin Woodman could not be found, Dorothy presses for clarity, asking directly, "What do you mean?" rather than letting the mystery pass unaddressed.

## Relationships

**[[Ozma]]** — friend. Seated together amid the assembled company in the palace drawing-room, with a chair kept vacant for her beside Ozma, their bond seems to reflect a companionship maintained through the events at Ev's court.

**[[BILLINA]]** — friend. Dorothy explicitly calls Billina 'my friend' and forbids the Hungry Tiger from ever eating her under any circumstances.

**[[Scarecrow]]** — friend. Their relationship seems to include ordinary companionship, as Dorothy is described spending most of an afternoon talking with the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman.

**[[Nome King]]** — enemy. An exchange referencing 'You cheated him, though' suggests a history of conflict or grievance between them.

**[[Tiktok]]** — employment. Tiktok describes himself as 'the slave of the girl Dor-oth-y, who res-cued me from pris-on', indicating that Dorothy freed him from imprisonment and that he considers himself bound to her service.

## Trivia

- When forbidding the Hungry Tiger from ever eating Billina, Dorothy uses the phrase "under any circ'mstances," a shortened turn of speech distinctive to how she talks.
- Dorothy carries Billina cradled in her arms rather than in a cage or basket; the hen is described as nestling closer in Dorothy's arms after being reassured she is safe from the Tiger.

contributions.title: Dorothy and the Wizard in Oz

page.title: DOROTHY
page.content:
## Biography

Dorothy is a girl whose home lies on a farm in Kansas, where she lives with her Uncle Henry and Aunt Em. When an earthquake struck and swallowed her from view, Uncle Henry and Aunt Em believed her killed and dressed in mourning, until Dorothy later found, through an enchanted picture, that they had returned to the farm still grieving her loss.

Her travels take her through a series of underground and enchanted regions in the company of the Wizard, a boy named Zeb, the horse Jim, and her kitten Eureka. In the Valley of Voe, pursued by unseen bears, the group escapes by rubbing the leaves of a strange plant on their feet and paws — the Wizard applying a leaf to Dorothy's shoes before treating his own, and Dorothy in turn rubbing a leaf on Eureka's paws — allowing them to walk safely out across the surface of a river.

During that crossing, Dorothy remained seated in the buggy with Eureka held in her arms while the Wizard drew it out onto the water, and Zeb ran across the river's surface toward her once he and Jim broke free of their unseen attackers.

Dorothy later becomes a guest of Princess Ozma in the Land of Oz, where the two spend days in festivity and companionship, Ozma valuing her company as a girl of her own age. On the third morning after Dorothy's arrival, she sat with Ozma and their friends in a reception room, talking over old times.

When Ozma's white piglet went missing from her boudoir, a maid reported that Dorothy's kitten had been seen slipping out of the room and running up the stairs. Hearing this, Dorothy and the Wizard exchanged startled glances, recalling how often Eureka had longed to eat a piglet.

## Narrative role

Dorothy arrives by train at Hugson's Siding, where she meets Zeb, who drives her toward Hugson's Ranch in a buggy drawn by the horse [[Jim]]. An earthquake soon splits the earth beneath them, and Dorothy, Zeb, Jim, and the buggy fall into a great crack leading deep underground. Underground, Dorothy and the Wizard pick the ripe Royal Princess from the Royal Bush, and this Princess deposes the reigning Prince to become the new ruler of the Mangaboos; the new Princess spares Dorothy, Zeb, and the Wizard but condemns Jim, Eureka, and the piglets to be driven into the Black Pit in the mountain. Dorothy, Zeb, and the Wizard then resist eating the invisibility-granting dama-fruit, learn that they must cross toward Pyramid Mountain to continue their journey, and receive an offer of help from an unseen ally confronting the bear threat there.

Continuing their escape, Dorothy joins the Wizard, Zeb, Jim, and Eureka in evading invisible bears in the Valley of Voe, walking on water after rubbing magic leaves upon their feet. At four o'clock Dorothy signals Ozma, who uses the Magic Belt to whisk her, then the rest of the group, to the Emerald City.

In the Emerald City, Ozma's white piglet disappears from her boudoir, and Dorothy's kitten Eureka is seen fleeing the room, casting suspicion on the kitten. Afterward, Dorothy and Zeb say farewell to Oz: Dorothy returns to Kansas, while Zeb and Jim return to Hugson's Ranch.

## Personality

Dorothy acts quickly to protect those around her: once the Wizard discovers the leaf that lets them walk on water, she immediately rubs it onto her kitten's paws so the animal can escape too, extending the remedy to a companion rather than keeping the advantage for herself. When Ozma's piglet goes missing, she and the Wizard "exchange startled glances," her alarm sharpening at once into suspicion as she recalls how often Eureka had longed to eat a piglet — a reaction that points to a watchful, quick-thinking mind. Her loyalty to her own family surfaces when the enchanted picture shows her that Uncle Henry and Aunt Em believe her dead: she responds "anxiously," insisting she "must get back as soon as poss'ble" to them. She is also described as "sweet and gentle and innocent," and as someone "the little ones all love" — an endearing presence among those who know her.

## Appearance

Excerpts refer to Dorothy as "the girl" and, elsewhere, as "the child," marking her as young rather than adult. No further physical description is given in the excerpts.

## Powers

Dorothy has no powers or abilities of her own. When escape from the invisible bears of the Valley of Voe demanded a way to cross open water, it was the Wizard who rubbed a leaf from a strange plant onto the soles of her shoes — not any innate gift of hers — that let her cross the river's surface without sinking, seated safely in the buggy with Eureka in her arms.

## Relationships

**[[WIZARD]]** — their bond seems to be one of friendship, reflected when he tells her "I remember you very well."

**[[Eureka]]** — her kitten, carried in her arms as they cross the river to escape the invisible bears; the bond suggests close friendship, evident when Dorothy calls out in distress, "Come back, Eureka!"

**[[Zeb]]** — the two appear to share a friendly connection, hinted at in the remark that "we must be second cousins."

**[[Princess Ozma]]** — Dorothy calls her "my friend the Princess Ozma," suggesting friendship; Ozma is said to be happy to have Dorothy beside her, since girls of her own age with whom it was proper for the Princess to associate were very few.

**[[Uncle Henry]]** — described as family, an impression reinforced by his own remark that "Eureka" means "I have found it"; upon learning through the enchanted picture that he and Aunt Em believed her killed by the earthquake, Dorothy anxiously says, "I must get back as soon as poss'ble to my own folks."

## Trivia

- Dorothy's white kitten, thought to be responsible for Ozma's missing white piglet, was seen fleeing Ozma's boudoir after the piglet disappeared.

## Biography

Dorothy is a traveler making her way toward the Land of Oz in the company of the shaggy man, Button-Bright, and Polly, the Rainbow's Daughter. When the shaggy man reads aloud a sign warning of the Destroying Sands bordering Oz, Dorothy confirms she has seen this desert before and that no one can survive walking upon it. Faced with the impossibility of crossing on foot and no way back, she admits she does not know what to do next, growing despondent at the group's predicament.

Dorothy recalls that magic has carried her to Oz and back on several occasions: a cyclone once carried her house there, after which a pair of Silver Shoes brought her home again in half a second, and on another occasion Ozma brought her over on her Magic Carpet while the Nome King's Magic Belt later took her home. She observes that magic accounted for every one of these journeys except the first, and that a cyclone cannot simply be relied upon to appear and carry the group to the Emerald City now. She travels with her dog Toto, held in her arms, and the shaggy man tells Johnny Dooit that Dorothy has friends in the Emerald City who will care for the travelers and see them safely home.

## Relationships

**[[Button-Bright]]** — friend. Their shared uncertainty at the desert's edge suggests a close bond: when Button-Bright wonders aloud what to do next, Dorothy answers just as helplessly, "I'm sure I don't know, either."

**[[THE shaggy man]]** — friend. Dorothy and THE shaggy man seem to travel as trusted companions; when he reads aloud the warning against the Deadly Sands, she confirms she has seen the desert before, and together they agree they mustn't try to cross it.

**[[Ozma]]** — friend. Dorothy's account of being carried to Oz by Ozma's Magic Carpet suggests a friendly connection between them, though the nature of that bond goes unstated here.

**[[Polly]]** — friend. Dorothy and Polly appear to share an easy rapport, exchanging questions about magic and rainbow-dancing; Dorothy gently declines Polly's invitation, noting other things "would suit me better than dancing on rainbows."

**[[Toto]]** — friend. Dorothy keeps Toto close, holding him in her arms as they cross the desert together in the sand-boat, suggesting a companionship between them.

## Biography

Dorothy, also known as Princess Dorothy, travels through the Land of Oz alongside a group of companions that includes the Wizard, Uncle Henry, the Shaggy Man, and Omby Amby. She and her fellow travelers ride away from the Cuttenclip village along an indistinct path until reaching a sign-post marking the main road, where the group continues pleasantly through pretty farming country. At a fork in the road, a sign-post reading "THIS WAY TO FUDDLECUMJIG" prompts Dorothy to observe that this is where they turn. During these travels she rides a horse made entirely of wood, one that never gets tired nor cares to lie down; Dorothy herself is not quite sure whether it ever sleeps, though it is certain the horse never does so when anyone is around.

Along the road, Dorothy inquires what the Flutterbudgets are like, though she is told it is no trouble to find places if one keeps to the right road. When a poor man they encounter cries out in distress after pricking his finger with a needle and seeing blood, Dorothy follows the Wizard, Uncle Henry, the Shaggy Man, and Omby Amby to his assistance as quickly as she can, and asks what has happened.

According to her own account, given after she, Toto, and Billina return to the signpost camp where the rest of the party has waited anxiously through the day tracking her footprints, Dorothy reports having eaten a wheelbarrow and a piano and having lunched with a King, a claim that leaves Aunt Em doubtful. In recounting her day to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, she describes visits to Utensia, Bunbury, and Bunnybury, though this account reflects Dorothy's own perspective rather than confirmed fact.

The travelers' route later takes them through Flutterbudget Center, where the residents are said to work themselves into panic over dangers that never come to pass, before reaching the Winkie Country, where Dorothy's party lunches with the Tin Woodman at his tin castle and tours his tin gardens and fish pond.

## Narrative role

Dorothy, traveling with Toto and Billina, returns to the signpost camp, where the Wizard's party has spent the day anxiously waiting after tracking her footprints there. Back among the group, she announces that she is not hungry, having already eaten a wheelbarrow and a piano and lunched with a King — a claim that leaves Aunt Em disbelieving.

She goes on to recount her day's adventures to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, describing her visits to Utensia, Bunbury, and Bunnybury. As the journey continues, she and the Wizard discuss airships, and the Wizard reveals that he is working on a magic recipe meant to keep airships from ever reaching the Land of Oz.

Later, Dorothy's party passes through Flutterbudget Center, where the residents work themselves into panic over hypothetical dangers that never occur.

Afterward, Glinda the Good casts a spell rendering all of Oz invisible to outsiders, and Dorothy sends a farewell note confirming that Oz is now cut off from the rest of the world forever.

## Personality

Dorothy shows marked curiosity about unfamiliar places and people, asking directly what the Flutterbudgets are like when she has never encountered them before. She is also observant, noticing and reading the sign-post that redirects the party toward Fuddlecumjig before anyone else remarks on it.

When Uncle Henry falls and the others rush to help him, Dorothy follows as quickly as she can, indicating a readiness to respond when someone in her company is in distress. She also presses further when the injured man's account seems incomplete, asking what has truly happened rather than accepting the first explanation — a small but consistent trait of wanting to understand a situation fully before moving on.

## Relationships

**[[Ozma]]** — friend. The pair travel together through the farming country beyond Cuttenclip, and it was Ozma who laid out the trip and "'vised" Dorothy's party to see the Rigmaroles next, which could indicate a trusted bond between them.

**[[Aunt Em]]** — family. Dorothy addresses her directly as "Aunt Em" during their journey together, as when she laughingly tells her, "I can't say 'zactly, Aunt Em, what they are," a familiarity that suggests a family tie.

**[[Billina]]** — friend. Billina travels at Dorothy's side, marching with her and Toto in the center of the spoon brigade at Utensia, which seems to point to a close companionship.

**[[Wizard]]** — friend. The Wizard journeys with Dorothy's party and rushes to help alongside her when trouble arises on the road, with Dorothy following "as quickly as she could," suggesting the two are allies within the traveling group.

**[[Toto]]** — friend. Toto stays close to Dorothy throughout the journey, accompanying her and Billina at the center of the spoon brigade's hollow square, which could indicate a steady, loyal companionship between them.

## Trivia

- Dorothy is unsure whether her wooden horse, the Sawhorse, ever sleeps, since it never seems to do so when anyone is nearby.

page.title: Toto
page.content:
## Biography

Toto is a small dog and constant companion of Dorothy on her journey through the forest toward the Emerald City. He walks close to her side through the woods, sensing threats — a deep growl from a hidden animal — before the rest of the group does. Those around him call him a "poor little dog" and a "brave little dog," descriptions borne out when he faces creatures far larger than himself.

When a Lion bounds into the road, Toto runs barking toward it despite the danger, prompting Dorothy to intervene and strike the Lion's nose to protect him. Later, when the Wicked Witch of the West strikes him with her umbrella, Toto flies at her and bites her leg in return. At other times his safety depends on his companions: the Tin Woodman catches and holds him when he jumps at a group of field mice, and Dorothy carries him in her arms across a ditch on the Lion's back and while poling the raft across the river.

Toto shares in the group's hardships and small comforts alike — eating what food is available, falling asleep among the poppies, and sleeping beside Dorothy at night while the Lion guards her door. In the Emerald City he is dressed for the occasion, a green ribbon and a small bell fastened around his neck to match Dorothy's green attire; when the travelers later leave the city, the ribbon loses its green color and turns white along with Dorothy's dress.

Toto retains habits from his life in Kansas, where he had always loved to chase mice, and does so again upon waking among a group of field mice during the journey. Among the gifts the Winkies give the travelers before their departure, Toto and the Lion each receive a golden collar.

## Narrative role

Toto is Dorothy's small black dog, described as the one lively, cheerful presence in her life. When Aunt Em orders Dorothy to the storm cellar, Aunt Em climbs down first while Dorothy searches for Toto. Dorothy and Toto then ride inside the swirling house for hours as it is carried far away; during the flight Toto nearly falls through the trap door but is pulled to safety, after which Dorothy eventually falls asleep.

After the Witch of the North and the Munchkins depart, Dorothy begins her journey with Toto. She eats breakfast, gathers fruit, and gives Toto food and water before setting out, and the two travel along the road of yellow brick toward the Emerald City to seek the Great Oz. Joined by the Scarecrow, Dorothy, the Scarecrow, and Toto continue along an increasingly rough and broken stretch of the road.

When the Cowardly Lion confronts the group, Dorothy rushes forward and slaps the Lion's nose to protect Toto, calling him a coward. Later, the scent of poppies overpowers Dorothy, Toto, and the Cowardly Lion, putting them to sleep, while the Scarecrow and Tin Woodman remain unaffected. Afterward, Toto tries to chase a gathered group of mice, but the Tin Woodman restrains him and assures the frightened Queen that Toto will not be allowed to bite.

The Winged Monkeys carry Dorothy, Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion through the air to the gates of the Emerald City. Once there, Toto knocks over a screen, revealing that Oz is only a little old bald man, not a terrible being.

The group later travels south in good spirits, with the Cowardly Lion relieved to be out of the City and Toto chasing moths and butterflies along the way. As they continue, the Tin Woodman builds a ladder while Dorothy, the Cowardly Lion, and Toto rest after their long walk.

Toto's journey ends alongside Dorothy: he returns together with her, closing the arc that began on the road of yellow brick.

## Personality

Toto shows a sharp, instinctive alertness to danger that his human companions lack: he senses a growling predator hidden in the trees before anyone else notices, going quiet and pressing close to Dorothy's side rather than barking. That same alertness turns to open defiance when a threat becomes visible — he barks and rushes at the Lion that bounds into the road, and later flies at the Wicked Witch and bites her leg after she strikes him, undeterred by creatures many times his size.

Outside of danger, Toto is playful and easily delighted: the sight of a group of field mice sends him bounding after them in one bark of joy, a habit Dorothy notes he had already formed chasing mice back in Kansas. He is also thoroughly at ease among his companions, content to be carried, fed, and settled beside Dorothy at night, and quick to fall asleep — a trait that, in the scented field near the Emerald City, leaves him as vulnerable to the flowers' effect as anyone in the group.

## Appearance

Toto is consistently described as a little dog, called at different points "the poor little dog" and "the brave little dog." While staying in the Emerald City, a green ribbon fitted with a small bell was tied around his neck; once the travelers left the city, the ribbon lost its green color and turned white along with Dorothy's dress. Later, upon leaving the land of the Winkies, the Winkies gave Toto a golden collar, a gift he received alongside the Cowardly Lion.

## Powers

Toto shows a keener instinct for danger than his human companions. Walking through the dark forest, unseen predators growl among the trees; the sound makes Dorothy's heart race because she cannot place its source, but Toto recognizes it at once, staying close at her side rather than reacting with alarm. This instinctive awareness lets him register threats before they are seen, setting him apart from the rest of the group.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. Toto stays constantly at her side through the forest, sleeps beside her at night, and rides in her arms across the ditch, the raft, and the Lion's back; their closeness seems genuine, as it is noted that "Dorothy played with him, and loved him dearly."

**[[Cowardly Lion]]** — friend. The bond suggests loyalty rather than lasting rivalry: although "the great beast had opened his mouth to bite the dog," Dorothy's intervention halts the attack, and the two travel and rest together afterward without further conflict, suggesting an uneasy but real companionship.

**[[Queen]]** — acquaintance. Their encounter seems limited to a moment of wariness, as the Queen of the Mice asks "Are you sure he will not bite us?" before being reassured that "Toto shall not hurt you."

**[[Tin Woodman]]** — other. The Tin Woodman appears protective toward Toto, as suggested by an account in which "the Woodman promptly chopped off the branch and set the little dog free."

**[[Wicked Witch]]** — enemy. Open hostility seems evident from a direct clash, in which "the Witch struck Toto a blow with her umbrella and the brave little dog flew at her and bit her leg in return."

## Trivia

- Before arriving in this world, Toto lived in Kansas, where he had a habit of chasing mice — a habit that resurfaced when he leapt with delight into a gathering of field mice.
- Unlike the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, who are not made of flesh and so are untroubled by it, Toto can be overcome by sleep in a field of poppies.
- During the travelers' stay in the Emerald City, Toto wore a green ribbon fastened with a small bell around his neck; once they left the city, the ribbon lost its green color and turned white, matching Dorothy's dress.
- The Winkies of the Yellow Land of the West gave Toto a golden collar as a parting gift, the same gift given to the Lion.
- When the Wicked Witch of the West struck him with her umbrella, Toto responded by biting her leg.

## Biography

Toto is Dorothy's little black dog, well known among those who follow her adventures. During the events of this story, Toto remained in Kansas while Dorothy traveled to California, and so he was unable to join her when her journey began; she brought her kitten along in his place.

## Biography

Toto is a small dog who travels as a constant companion to Dorothy, staying close to her throughout the journey toward the Emerald City. When the shaggy man introduces Johnny Dooit to the group, Toto is named alongside Dorothy, Button-Bright, and the Rainbow's Daughter among the travelers stranded at the edge of the Deadly Desert. Toto rides in Dorothy's arms aboard the sand-boat Johnny Dooit builds, seated with her at the bottom of the vessel as it carries the group across the desert sands.

When the sand-boat crashes into the rocks at the desert's far edge, Toto is thrown into the air along with Dorothy, Button-Bright, and Polly, tumbling onto the grass beyond unharmed. Excited by the crash, Toto seizes one of the donkey's ears in his teeth, shaking and worrying it while growling angrily, until the shaggy man lands in a heap beside him.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. Toto stays at Dorothy's side throughout, carried in her arms as she boards the sand-boat, and the detail that "Toto wagged his tail as if he understood" suggests a bond of closeness and mutual understanding between them.

**[[Billina]]** — enemy. An episode in which Toto "flew at the yellow hen, who ruffled her feathers and let out such an angry screech" could indicate friction between the two, though the excerpts show only this brief clash rather than a lasting rivalry.

**[[Nick Chopper]]** — friend. A remark that the Emperor "was fond of Dorothy's little dog" suggests a measure of goodwill toward Toto, though no direct exchange between them appears in the excerpts.

## Biography

Toto is a small dog who travels at Dorothy's side. While marching through Utensia inside the hollow square formed by the Spoon Brigade, Toto walks with Dorothy and Billina at the center and knocks over one of the spoons by wagging his tail, prompting the Captain of the Spoons to warn the little dog to be more careful. Approaching a village, Toto barks loudly at a large beetle crossing the path, setting off a wild clatter from the houses and yards. On a later, anxious night, Toto walks by Dorothy's side, his spirits subdued. A note signed in Dorothy's voice states that Toto and she will always love the one it is addressed to, suggesting a close bond between the two.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. Toto stays close to her throughout her travels, which seems to reflect a bond of companionship.

**[[Billina]]** — friend. Their shared presence in the traveling party suggests a friendly rapport.

**[[Mr. Bunn]]** — enemy. Their appearance together could indicate some friction, though the excerpts do not make this explicit.

## Infobox

- Name: Emerald City
- Place type: City
- Region: Land of Oz
- Ruler: The Scarecrow (formerly Oz, the Great and Terrible)
- Status: Active

## Biography

The Emerald City lies within the Land of Oz, in the country where the Great Oz dwells, and is reached by following the road of yellow brick. The Tin Woodman once said he had never been there himself, though his father had made the journey and described it as a long passage through a dangerous country, while the country nearer the city is beautiful. Travelers approaching from the east had to cross a broad river and a deadly poppy field before reaching a smooth, well-paved stretch of the road leading directly to the city.

Access to the Emerald City is controlled through a great gate, opened only after ringing a bell, by the Guardian of the Gates. Before granting entry, the Guardian leads visitors into his room and locks a pair of spectacles from a great box onto their eyes; these are unlocked and returned to the box when the visitors leave. Within, the streets of the city lead to the Palace of Oz, where the Great Oz himself dwelt.

## Appearance

According to Oz, the city and the country around it were so green and beautiful that he named it the Emerald City, and to make the name fit better he had green spectacles locked onto the eyes of everyone who entered, so that everything they saw appeared green. This was borne out when a departing traveler's ribbon, green throughout the visit, lost that color and turned white as soon as the spectacles were removed and the Emerald City was left behind.

## Events

Dorothy and Toto first set out along the road of yellow brick toward the Emerald City to seek the Great Oz, and the party renewed this journey more than once after delays — a night spent on a riverbank, during which Dorothy dreamed of the city and of the Wizard, and being swept downriver past the road itself. After finding the road of yellow brick again, the travelers reached the city's great gate, where the Guardian of the Gates locked spectacles onto their eyes before leading them through streets that appeared green in every particular, and a crowd gathered to follow them to the Palace of Oz. Later, having taken the Golden Cap from the Wicked Witch's cupboard and received parting gifts from the Winkies, the companions set out again for the Emerald City to claim Oz's promises, but lost their way among fields of buttercups and daisies. Dorothy then read the charm inside the Golden Cap to summon the Winged Monkeys, who carried Dorothy, Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Lion through the air straight to the city's gates.

## Trivia

- Oz stated that he ordered the city and his Palace built to amuse himself and keep the people occupied, and that they did the work willingly and well.
- After Oz's departure, the Scarecrow became ruler of the Emerald City and its Palace; the people took pride in the fact that no other city in the world was ruled by a stuffed man.
- The people continued to remember Oz as their friend, crediting him with having built the Emerald City and the Palace before leaving the Scarecrow to rule in his place.

## Biography

The Emerald City, also known simply as the City, is the seat of royal power where His Majesty the Scarecrow reigns, having been invited by its people to rule them, just as the Winkies invited the Tin Woodman to become their own ruler. Its inhabitants speak the language of the Munchkins, which is also the language of the Emerald City. Tip believed the road he and Jack Pumpkinhead followed led south toward the Emerald City, though he admitted he was not entirely sure of the direction. A yellow brick road, marked partway by a sign reading nine miles to the city, leads travelers to its gates.

## Events

Tip and Jack Pumpkinhead, learning that the Scarecrow now rules the Emerald City, set out together to reach it, camping along the yellow brick road on the way. Jack, riding the Saw-Horse, outpaces Tip and arrives first at the green wall marking the city's edge; a Soldier with Green Whiskers then leads Jack and the Saw-Horse through the emerald streets to the royal palace, where Jack meets His Majesty the Scarecrow. Tip, following on foot and growing hungry after finishing his rations, later reaches the city himself, where he encounters General Jinjur, leader of an all-girl Army of Revolt marching to conquer the Emerald City and take the throne from the Scarecrow. Jinjur declares the city has been ruled by men long enough and wants its gems and treasury for her army, tired of male rule. The invading army enters the city, its soldiers pausing to dig emeralds from the walls and paving-stones with the points of their knitting-needles before reaching the palace. Learning of the conquest, the Tin Woodman, addressed as Emperor, resolves to march at once and recapture the Emerald City so the Scarecrow may be placed again upon his throne.

## Appearance

The Emerald City is enclosed by a green wall, the first sight travelers meet upon approach. Its streets are described as emerald streets, and both its walls and paving-stones are set with emeralds, valuable enough that invading soldiers pried them loose with knitting-needles. According to the Scarecrow, everything within the Emerald City is green, in contrast to the purple of the Gillikin country, the blue of the Munchkin country, the red of the Quadling country in the south, and the yellow of the Winkie country in the west.

## Trivia

- A sign along the yellow brick road reads nine miles to the Emerald City.
- The Scarecrow himself remarks that ruling the Emerald City is a tiresome job and that his crown is heavy enough to give him a headache.
- General Jinjur claims the King's treasury holds enough money to buy every girl in her Army a dozen new gowns.

## Infobox

- Name: Emerald City
- Place type: Town
- Region: Center of the four kingdoms of the Land of Oz
- Status: Active

## Biography

The Emerald City is the town where Ozma, supreme ruler of the Land of Oz, lives, standing in the exact center of the four kingdoms — those of the Munchkins, the Winkies, the Quadlings, and the Gillikins — each governed by its own king under her rule. A road of yellow brick leads straight to its jewel-studded gates. When Ozma and her companions returned there, the Munchkin king had escorted them to its border, and the people turned out everywhere to greet Ozma and to hail the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion as popular favorites. The Cowardly Lion, ruler of the great forest as King of Beasts, journeyed to the Emerald City to see Ozma after she became reigning princess.

## Events

Ozma's party, including Dorothy, Tiktok, and Billina, crosses the desert on a magic carpet on their way to the Emerald City, meeting Jinjur — now a contented farm wife — along the way.

## Biography

The Emerald City is a city in Oz, formerly ruled by the Wizard before he "went up in a balloon" and escaped, after which Dorothy got back to Kansas by means of a pair of magical silver shoes. On a later return, Jellia Jamb greets the visitors but tells the Wizard he cannot rule the Emerald City as he used to, because the people now have "a beautiful Princess whom everyone loves dearly," and a Captain-General adds that the people will not willingly part with her. The city's people are described as so well-behaved that there was not a single lawyer among them, and it had been years since any Ruler had sat in judgment upon an offender of the law — until the arrest and trial of Eureka. Ozma keeps a palace in the city, in whose apartments she carries her own piglet after the Wizard returns it to her.

## Events

When news of Eureka's arrest and trial becomes known, tremendous excitement prevails in the Emerald City. After the trial, Ozma gives the Wizard back the piglet he had allowed Nick Chopper to substitute for the lost one, and the citizens of the Emerald City scatter to their homes, well content with the day's amusement. Dorothy also signals Ozma, who uses the Magic Belt to whisk her, then the rest of the group, to the Emerald City.

## Biography

The Emerald City lies within the Land of Oz and is the destination Dorothy seeks when she wishes to cross the desert separating her from Oz. She has crossed that desert to reach the city more than once before, though by magical means each time — carried over by Ozma's Magic Carpet on one occasion, and returned home by the Nome King's Magic Belt on another. Dorothy notes that magic accomplished the crossing every time except the first. The Shaggy Man and his companions likewise set out anxious to reach the Emerald City, since Dorothy has friends there who would take care of the travelers and send them safely home again.

## Appearance

The Emerald City is separated from outside lands by a desert whose sands turn any living flesh that touches them into dust, making the crossing itself perilous and effectively impassable without aid.

## Events

On the way toward the Emerald City, the traveling group is met by Tik-tok and Billina, who guide them onward and lead them to stop overnight at Nick Chopper's tin castle. Later, the Cowardly Lion and the Hungry Tiger meet the party bearing Ozma's golden chariot, escorting them the rest of the way into the Emerald City and into the royal palace itself.

## Trivia

- The desert surrounding the Emerald City turns all living flesh that touches it into dust, making it a barrier that ordinary travel cannot overcome.
- Dorothy reached the city safely on past occasions only through magical aid — Ozma's Magic Carpet and the Nome King's Magic Belt among the means used.

## Biography

The Emerald City stands within the Land of Oz, on the far side of the Deadly Desert from the mountains beneath which the Nome King keeps his extensive caverns. It is home to Ozma and to the Wizard of Oz, who was to live in the Emerald City always, as Glinda the Sorceress had arranged. The Tin Woodman, addressed as Emperor, had likewise spent a long residence in the Emerald City before his tastes turned again to farm life, and Jack Pumpkinhead once lived there with Ozma.

At one point the Nome King, under King Roquat and his adviser Guph, was secretly driving a tunnel through solid rock beneath the Deadly Desert, extending it toward the walls of the Emerald City so that an army of Nomes — to be joined by the Whimsies, the Growleywogs, and the Phanfasms — could march through it and attack Oz.

## Appearance

The Emerald City is enclosed by walls, the same walls toward which the Nome King's tunnel was being extended.

## Events

A visit to the Scarecrow's corn-shaped mansion and to Jack Pumpkinhead's pumpkin farm ends with both agreeing to travel to the Emerald City to support Ozma.

## Trivia

- Guph considers the conquest of Oz assured once the Whimsies, the Growleywogs, and the Phanfasms join the Nome King's forces.

## Infobox

- Place type: Prairie
- Status: Unreachable from the Land of Oz by any known route

## Biography

Kansas is the home of Dorothy, who lives there with her guardians, Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, in a small house on the prairies. Her dog Toto also lived there before arriving in the Land of Oz, and had been accustomed to chasing mice while at home. From the moment Dorothy arrives in Oz, she repeatedly states her wish to return to Kansas, calling it her home even though she cannot say exactly where it lies — when a man asks her where Kansas is, she admits she does not know, only that it is her home and that she is sure it exists somewhere. According to the Munchkins and the Witch, deserts block every direction out of the country and none of them can be crossed, and even Oz himself confesses he has no idea which way Kansas lies, saying it will take more than imagination to carry Dorothy back there. When Dorothy later asks the Winged Monkeys to fly her to Kansas, their King refuses.

## Appearance

Kansas is described as gray, a description Dorothy draws in contrast to the beauty of the country she finds herself in after arriving in Oz.

## Events

Dorothy lives with Uncle Henry and Aunt Em in a small house on the gray Kansas prairies before her arrival in Oz. Once in Oz, she asks how to get home, only to be told that deserts block every direction and none can be crossed. She explains to the Scarecrow why she wants to return to gray Kansas despite the beauty of the land she is in. She decides to ask Oz to send her home, just as the Scarecrow wishes for brains and the Tin Woodman for a heart, and each companion in turn states the same wishes before Oz. Oz eventually promises to find a way to send her back, though left alone he privately admits to himself that he does not know how it can be done. Afterward, when the four companions meet again, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Lion each express contentment with what they gained from Oz, while Dorothy alone insists she still wants to return to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry in Kansas.

## Trivia

- A man Dorothy meets is surprised to learn of Kansas at all, asking "Where is Kansas?" as though the place is unknown to him.
- Dorothy notes that Omaha, where the Wizard says he was born, is not very far from Kansas, though the Wizard replies that it is "farther from here."

## Biography

Kansas is a farm region and the home of Dorothy, her Uncle Henry, and her Aunt Em. Dorothy states she was born on a farm in Kansas. On one occasion, after traveling to Oz and becoming separated from her companions, she got back to Kansas by means of a pair of magical silver shoes. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em remain at the farm in Kansas during Dorothy's travels; through an enchanted picture, Dorothy once saw that Uncle Henry had returned to the farm in Kansas, and that both he and Aunt Em were dressed in mourning, believing their niece had been killed by an earthquake. Dorothy considers herself bound to the farm, explaining she cannot be away for long because Uncle Henry and Aunt Em need her help.

## Events

Dorothy returns to Kansas after bidding farewell to Oz, while her companions Zeb and Jim return instead to Hugson's Ranch.

## Trivia

- While Dorothy travels in California, her dog Toto remains in Kansas.
- Uncle Henry and Dorothy plan to travel back to Kansas after being away from home for a long time.

## Biography

Kansas is the home of Dorothy, who is repeatedly referred to as "the little Kansas girl." It exists as a point of comparison for the wonders of Oz: when praising the skill of the Winkie tinsmiths who built a castle, the shaggy man remarks that "it would be hard to match this castle in Kansas," suggesting that Kansas construction does not rival the craftsmanship found among the Winkies.

## Events

Following Ozma's birthday celebration, which draws many guests to the palace and its grounds, the Wizard sends several visitors home by magic bubbles, while Dorothy returns to Kansas using the Magic Belt.

## Trivia

- Dorothy is twice identified by others as "the little Kansas girl," a phrase used both by Jack Pumpkinhead's greeter and in her own joyful exclamation upon reuniting with the Hungry Tiger.

## Biography

Kansas is a place in the United States and is Dorothy's home. Dorothy has stated that she used to live in Kansas, in the United States, and that she has also been to California and Australia, as has Uncle Henry. Using her magic picture, Ozma has watched Dorothy in her Kansas home, and once did so again while Dorothy and her companions were occupied at Fuddlecumjig, laughing merrily at the scene. Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, associated with Dorothy, are likewise connected to Kansas: Aunt Em recalls the flies of Kansas as unwilling to behave unless swatted, unlike the more agreeable flies of Oz, and Uncle Henry has traveled from there to California and Australia as well.

Kansas is also spoken of as a possible destination reachable from Oz by means of the Magic Belt, raising the idea of escape from danger by returning there, with the suggestion that Ozma might be brought along and supported through the group's work so she would not be left alone and unhappy over the loss of her fairy country.

## Events

When faced with the destruction of her fairy country, Ozma refuses to fight or flee, rejecting plans to arm the Winkies or to escape to Kansas by means of the Magic Belt, choosing instead to share the fate of her people.

## Trivia

- A picture puzzle craze once took place in Kansas, giving Dorothy experience matching puzzles with flat pictures.
- According to Aunt Em, the flies of Kansas do not understand anything but a swat, unlike the politely-behaved flies of Oz; the same is said to hold true for mosquitoes.
- When the question of finding work in Kansas for the Tin Woodman was raised, Uncle Henry suggested that, being hollow, he might be used in a canning factory.

page.title: Aunt Em
page.content:
## Biography

Aunt Em is the wife of Uncle Henry, a farmer, and Dorothy's aunt. She lives with him on the Kansas prairies, in a small house built from lumber hauled by wagon over many miles — a single room holding a cookstove, a cupboard, a table, a few chairs, and the beds, along with a dug-out cyclone cellar where the family could shelter from the great whirlwinds that could crush the building. When Aunt Em first came to live there she was a young, pretty wife, but the sun and wind of the prairie changed her over the years, much as they grayed the house and the land around it.

Throughout Dorothy's time away, Aunt Em remains constantly in her niece's thoughts: Dorothy repeatedly voices her wish to return to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, worries that Aunt Em will be dreadfully anxious over her long absence, and fears Aunt Em may believe something terrible has befallen her. When Dorothy finally makes her way home, she finds Aunt Em outside the house watering the cabbages; seeing Dorothy running toward her, Aunt Em calls out, "My darling child!" and welcomes her back.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — family. Aunt Em shares the small Kansas farmhouse with Dorothy, and the available context suggests Dorothy first came to live with her as an orphan; Dorothy repeatedly names her among the people she most wants to return to, and upon arriving home Aunt Em rushes out to greet her, crying "My darling child!"

**[[Uncle Henry]]** — family. Excerpts identify Aunt Em as "the farmer's wife," sharing the same one-room house and bed with Uncle Henry; the available context hints she is spoken of as his wife, consistent with Dorothy naming them together whenever she longs for home.

page.title: Aunt Em
page.content:
## Biography

Aunt Em travels with Dorothy, Uncle Henry, and the Wizard through the Land of Oz, encountering many oddities she does not fully understand. Skeptical of unfamiliar things, she remarks that "no one would suspect it from their name" upon hearing of an unfamiliar group, and later wonders whether they are "more paper things." When a kangaroo cries inconsolably, she suggests "it must be her mince-pie," a guess Uncle Henry answers with his own, "or her milk-toast." Invited to lunch with the Tin Woodman, she asks with some apprehension, "Must we lunch on tin?", and Dorothy reassures her that Nick Chopper will provide "plenty of good things to eat." At the Tin Woodman's castle she remains wary of local hazards, inquiring whether he keeps "any Flutterbudgets or Rigmaroles," and comments dryly on the castle's spotless tin surfaces, supposing "they polish their Emperor, too."

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — family. Dorothy addresses her directly as "Aunt Em" and admits she "can't say 'zactly" what lies ahead, an exchange that suggests a close, familial closeness; according to Dorothy's own account of her day, Aunt Em also reacts with disbelief on hearing her adventures.

**[[Uncle Henry]]** — family. Their paired banter — she guesses a crying kangaroo's trouble is "her mince-pie," and he counters with "Or her milk-toast" — suggests a familial rapport, though the excerpts do not spell out its exact nature.

**[[Wizard]]** — acquaintance. He answers one of her questions with "No one, madam," a reply that suggests a cordial but formal acquaintance rather than close familiarity.

**[[Billina]]** — friendly_rivalry. She is said to have gotten "into an argument with Billina about the proper way to raise chickens," an exchange that suggests good-natured rivalry rather than real hostility.

**[[Nick Chopper]]** — acquaintance. She asks uneasily, "Must we lunch on tin?" and later inquires whether he keeps "any Flutterbudgets or Rigmaroles at his castle," questions that suggest wary curiosity about him rather than familiarity.

## Biography

Glinda is the Good Witch who rules the South Country, known there as the Witch of the South. Her castle stands on the edge of the desert, and the Quadlings consider her good, saying she is kind to everyone. She receives visitors seated on a throne of rubies within her castle, where Dorothy and her companions present themselves after tidying themselves. To Dorothy and her companions she appears both beautiful and young. When Dorothy recounts her story and asks to return to Kansas, Glinda agrees to help her, asking in exchange for the Golden Cap, which Dorothy willingly gives up.

page.title: Glinda the Good
page.content:
## Biography

Glinda the Good, also known simply as Glinda, is the Sorceress who rules the Quadlings of the South Country. She resides in a palace set within gorgeous gardens, where a fountain sends sprays of gems instead of water into a carved marble basin, and where a company of girl soldiers stands guard. As the owner of the Golden Cap, she commands the services of the Winged Monkeys, who are said to be her slaves. When Tip and his companions seek advice, the Scarecrow describes her as "a very delightful Queen" who would gladly receive them, and Nick Chopper vouches that he knows her and believes she will prove a friend.

Glinda's Army, gathered at daybreak before her palace gates in uniforms of gay colors and armed with silver-tipped spears, marches toward the Emerald City. By night the forces silently surround the city and pitch tents of scarlet silk upon the greensward around Glinda's own tent of pure white silk hung with scarlet banners. When Queen Jinjur's messenger comes to ask her demands, Glinda requires that Mombi be surrendered to her.

## Relationships

**[[Old Mombi]]** — enemy. Glinda marches her army to the Emerald City and demands that Mombi be surrendered to her, suggesting an adversarial relationship between them.

**[[Nick Chopper]]** — friend. Nick Chopper says he knows Glinda the Good and believes she will prove "a friend indeed."

**[[The Scarecrow]]** — ally. The Scarecrow speaks warmly of her, calling her "a very delightful Queen" and proposing to seek her advice.

**[[General Jinjur]]** — enemy. Jinjur's soldiers are alarmed at the sight of Glinda's army surrounding the Emerald City, and Jinjur despairs that they are "surely lost," suggesting an adversarial relationship.

**[[Tip]]** — friend. Tip travels with the Scarecrow's party toward Glinda's palace to seek her counsel, suggesting a favorable connection between them.

page.title: Glinda the Good
page.content:
## Biography

Glinda the Good is a sorceress of Oz, described as a friendly sorceress of the land. When Ozma sought a way to cross the great desert separating Oz from the land of Ev, in order to free prisoners held there, she turned to Glinda, who at once presented her with a magic carpet that continually unrolled beneath their feet, making a path across the desert. Dorothy likewise turns to Glinda for help, confident that Glinda will assist her and advise her on how to reach Uncle Henry. When Ozma and Dorothy travel to see her, Glinda receives them graciously and listens to Dorothy's story with attention. Alongside Dorothy, Glinda helps Ozma defeat the Nome King's plan to capture the Emerald City.

## Relationships

**[[Ozma]]** — ally. Glinda presents Ozma with a magic carpet to help her cross the desert, which suggests an allied bond between the two.

**[[DOROTHY]]** — friend. Dorothy turns to Glinda for help and advice in reaching her Uncle Henry, hinting at a trusting friendship between them.

**[[Jinjur]]** — enemy. Jinjur is said to have once fought a battle against "the powerful army of Glinda the Sorceress," which could indicate a hostile history between them.

**[[Nome King]]** — enemy. Ozma and Dorothy, with Glinda's help, defeat the Nome King's plan to capture the Emerald City, suggesting an adversarial relationship.

page.title: Glinda the Good
page.content:
## Biography

Glinda the Good, known also as Glinda or the Sorceress, resides in a stately castle in the Land of Oz and is called the Good Sorceress. She keeps a Magic Book, through which she reads of travelers before they arrive, and she knows in advance when guests are coming to her castle.

Glinda is credited with placing a fountain whose water once cured a wicked king of his wickedness: after drinking from it, his mind became innocent and vacant, and when he relearned the things of life they were all good things.

She is also said to have made a city, doing so out of fondness for rabbits.

Glinda once taught the Wizard of Oz one of her tricks, magic he considered far better than what he had practiced in Omaha or when he first came to Oz. When she learned that the Wizard was to live in the Emerald City permanently, she promised to help him, holding that the Wizard of Oz ought to be a clever wizard and not a humbug; since then the two have spent much time together, with the Wizard learning quickly under her instruction. Among the events attributed to her is an occasion on which she worked a magic spell.

Dorothy counts herself acquainted with Glinda, remarking that she would ask her to put another King in a usurper's place.

## Narrative role

At a decisive turn, Glinda the Good works a magic spell that renders all of Oz invisible to outsiders, sealing the land off from any further contact with the world beyond it. Dorothy takes part in this closing act by sending a farewell note, which confirms that Oz is now cut off from the rest of the world forever.

This spell stands as Glinda's most consequential act: rather than settling a single dispute, her sorcery permanently changes the terms on which Oz exists in relation to everywhere else.

## Personality

Glinda is consistently described as benevolent, her epithet "the Good" attached to her name at every mention. Her magic is used to correct wrongs rather than to dominate: she placed an enchanted fountain so that a once-wicked King would drink of it, forget his cruelty, and become innocent and good again, showing a corrective, restorative bent to her power. Her generosity extends to small creatures as well as to kings — she built a city for rabbits simply because she was fond of them, suggesting an affection that is not limited to the great or powerful.

She is also principled about fairness in the exercise of authority: on learning that the Wizard would live in the Emerald City permanently, she resolved to help him become a genuinely clever Wizard rather than remain a humbug, implying she values earned competence over mere appearance of power. Toward guests she is warm and welcoming — she receives visitors "in her gracious way," having anticipated their arrival through her Magic Book, which points to a hospitable, attentive disposition rather than aloof mystique.

## Appearance

## Powers

Glinda the Good, also known as Glinda or the Sorceress, is a practitioner of true magic, distinguished from lesser trickery. She once placed a fountain whose water strips away wickedness: a wicked king who drank from it had his mind rendered innocent and vacant, so that when his understanding returned it held only good things. She has personally taught magic to the Wizard of Oz, passing on at least one trick described as better than what he had practiced before reaching Oz. She keeps a Magic Book, through which she can read of travelers and learn of their approach before they arrive. On one occasion she worked a magic spell that resolved a tense situation without anyone being hurt, judged by those present as preferable to fighting. She is also credited with creating a city said to have been made out of fondness for its rabbit inhabitants, though the extent of this claim rests on a single account.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — seems to be an ally of Glinda; when trapped as "It" by a King, Dorothy says she will ask Glinda to put another King in his place, suggesting she trusts Glinda's authority to intervene.

**[[Ozma]]** — appears allied with Glinda, suggested by a moment of gratitude toward her for a promise of assistance, though the exact circumstance is not detailed further.

**[[Aunt Em]]** — seems to be a passing acquaintance of Glinda, having asked with curiosity about her Magic Book.

**[[King]]** — Glinda's relationship to a King is unclear beyond her role in placing a fountain whose waters once cured a wicked King of his wickedness, which could indicate some authority over him.

**[[Wizard]]** — appears to have served as a mentor to the Wizard, who credits her with teaching him a magic trick more effective than what he practiced before coming to Oz.

## Trivia

- Glinda is said to have created a city out of her fondness for rabbits, building it for them as an act of favor.
- She keeps a Magic Book through which she can read of distant events, allowing her to know of visitors' approach before they arrive at her castle.

page.title: Uncle Henry
page.content:
## Biography

Uncle Henry is a farmer living on the great Kansas prairies with his wife, Aunt Em, and their niece Dorothy, an orphan who came to live with them. Their original house was small, built of lumber carried by wagon many miles, and contained a single room with a rusty cookstove, a cupboard, a table, a few chairs, and the beds, along with a dug-out cyclone cellar for shelter from the great whirlwinds that threatened the region. Years of hard labor marked him: he worked from morning till night and, according to the account of his household, never laughed and did not know what joy was.

After a cyclone carried away the old house, Uncle Henry built a new farmhouse on the same prairie land. He is later seen milking the cows in the barnyard of this new home. Dorothy repeatedly names him, together with Aunt Em, as the person she most wishes to return to, and she expresses worry that a poor harvest might leave him unable to afford the hardships of her prolonged absence.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — family. Uncle Henry lives with Dorothy on the Kansas prairies, and she names him alongside Aunt Em as the family she longs to return to throughout her time in Oz.

**[[Aunt Em]]** — family. Uncle Henry and Aunt Em share a home and a bed in one corner of their small house, with Dorothy in another corner nearby.

## Biography

Uncle Henry is Dorothy's uncle. While Dorothy travels through Oz and Ev, he is far away in Australia, having reached the country aboard his ship. In a vision Dorothy sees of him, he sits in an easy chair in a pleasant room in Sydney, solemnly smoking his briar pipe, his hair now quite white and his hands and face thin and wasted. Dorothy, watching him, believes his condition has worsened because he is worried about her prolonged absence.

## Biography

Uncle Henry is Dorothy's uncle and lives on a farm in Kansas. Dorothy travelled with him to Australia and afterward to San Francisco, before he went on to Hugson's Ranch for a visit while she stayed a few days in the city. Uncle Henry's wife's sister is married to Uncle Bill Hugson, the rancher Zeb works for, a connection Zeb describes as making them second cousins.

After Dorothy vanished, the enchanted picture in Ozma's palace showed that Uncle Henry had returned to the Kansas farm, dressed in mourning together with Aunt Em, believing their niece had been killed by the earthquake. Dorothy considers helping Uncle Henry and Aunt Em on the farm one of her responsibilities, saying she can never stay away from it for very long.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — family. The excerpts identify her as his niece, and this bond seems to explain why Dorothy, on seeing Uncle Henry and Aunt Em mourning her in the enchanted picture, insists she cannot stay long away from the farm, since he and Aunt Em need her help.

page.title: Uncle Henry
page.content:
## Biography

Uncle Henry is a member of the travelling party that accompanies Princess Dorothy through the Land of Oz, alongside the Wizard, Aunt Em, the Shaggy Man, and Omby Amby. Even amid the country's oddities, he keeps a good-humored, practical outlook, remarking to Aunt Em that "this is a queer country, and we may as well take people as we find them." When the group visited the Fuddles, he found the experience more entertaining than playing solitaire or mumbletypeg, and said he was glad they had gone. He is also quick to offer suggestions, wondering aloud whether the Wizard might know the way to a destination, and joking with the Tin Woodman that, being hollow, he might find work in a canning factory.

He is not merely an observer: when cries for help were heard along the road, Uncle Henry was among those — with the Wizard, the Shaggy Man, and Omby Amby — who jumped from the wagon and ran to the aid of the man in distress. During a visit to the Tin Woodman's tin castle, he and Aunt Em were bubbling over with admiration for the castle and its polished owner, so much that Dorothy set aside, for a time, her suspicion that something was troubling their host. According to Dorothy's account, Uncle Henry was also among those with whom she later shared the story of her day's visits to Utensia, Bunbury, and Bunnybury.

## Relationships

**[[Aunt Em]]** — family. Their domestic closeness comes through in small shared moments, such as Uncle Henry proposing her milk-toast, and their joint reaction of admiration at the Tin Woodman's castle.

**[[Dorothy]]** — family. A remark noting that he has "been to California and to Australia" alongside her suggests a shared personal history consistent with a familial bond, though the excerpts do not state the relation outright.

**[[Ozma]]** — employment. A mention of making Uncle Henry "the Keeper of the Jewels" could indicate some employment tie to Ozma, though it is not confirmed whether this ever took effect.

**[[Wizard]]** — ally. Their cooperation appears in his deference to the Wizard for guidance early on and in acting together, alongside the Shaggy Man and Omby Amby, to help a stranger in distress.

**[[Nick Chopper]]** — friend. Their exchange, in which Uncle Henry jokingly suggests the hollow Tin Woodman could work in a canning factory, hints at an easy familiarity between them.

## Infobox

- Name: Land of Oz
- Place type: Country
- Isolation: Cut off from the rest of the world, never civilized

## Biography

The Land of Oz is a country cut off from the rest of the world, a condition said to explain why witches and wizards still dwell there when, in the civilized countries, none are said to remain. Within its bounds live at least four witches: those of the North and South, described as good, and those of the East and West, described as wicked. After the Witch of the East is killed, only the Wicked Witch of the West remains as the land's sole remaining wicked witch. Regions of the Land of Oz are marked by distinct local dress; travelers nearing the Emerald City encounter people clothed in emerald-green and wearing peaked hats like those of the Munchkins. Dorothy is brought to the Land of Oz by a cyclone that carries her away from the gray country of Kansas, and she later recounts to the Witch how the cyclone brought her there and how she found her companions. Toto, who accompanies her, is said not to care whether he is in Kansas or the Land of Oz so long as Dorothy is with him.

## Events

On returning home, Dorothy tells Aunt Em that she has come from the Land of Oz.

## References

## Infobox

- Name: Land of Oz
- Place type: Country
- Regions: Country of the Gillikins, land of the Munchkins
- Ruler: Scarecrow (His Majesty)

## Biography

The Land of Oz is a country bordered by a wide, sandy desert that separates it from the rest of the world. Within its borders lie distinct regions, including the Country of the Gillikins in the north and the land of the Munchkins, recognizable by its blue houses and fences. Nearly all farm houses across the Land of Oz share a round, dome-shaped construction. At the time of these events, the Scarecrow holds the throne as His Majesty and is regarded as the wisest personage in the Land of Oz. His rule is challenged when General Jinjur assembles an army — a regiment of girls gathered from the four corners of the Land of Oz — to conquer him and seize the throne. Glinda the Good, described as a mighty Sorceress, is said to have such command of magic that nothing occurring anywhere in the Land of Oz escapes her notice.

## Events

The Gump, carrying a group of travelers, flies through the night and into the first streaks of dawn, bearing them beyond the borders of the Land of Oz into unfamiliar territory — rolling plains dotted with strange villages whose houses have slanting, peaked roofs rather than the dome shapes common throughout the Land of Oz.

## Appearance

The Land of Oz is described as being of small extent. Its farm houses are characteristically round and dome-shaped, a detail travelers note is unique to the country once they cross beyond it into unfamiliar lands where houses instead have peaked roofs. The country is enclosed by a wide, sandy desert, marking the boundary with the outside world.

## Trivia

- No bug in all the Land of Oz had reportedly ever attained the size of the Woggle-Bug encountered by the Scarecrow's company.
- Beyond the sandy desert bordering the Land of Oz lies what is called the terrible outside world.

- Region: across the desert from the Land of Oz, bordered to the north by a great mountain

## Biography

The Land of Ev is a kingdom whose royal family was held in long imprisonment, their liberation being the stated purpose of Ozma's expedition there. The country lies beyond a dangerous desert from the Land of Oz, a stretch crossed by means of a magic carpet. Its landscape includes a valley lying between two high mountains, with a third great mountain blocking the valley and forming the northern edge of Ev; the Nome King's palace was said to lie underneath that mountain. After the royal family's release, the new King of Ev pledged his gratitude to Ozma and promised to render the Land of Oz any service within his power.

## Events

Despite the power of a magic belt, a rescue party was unable to locate the Tin Woodman while in Ev and was forced to depart without him, returning to the Land of Ev with the rescued royal family.

## Infobox

- Name: Land of Oz
- Ruler: Princess Ozma

## Biography

The Land of Oz is a marvelous country, reached by travelers such as the Wizard and Dorothy after passing through many queer countries in their travels. Access to Oz is tied to the Magic Belt, by which Princess Ozma can bring travelers to herself in the Land of Oz once a sign is given. Within Oz stands a palace containing an enchanted picture, through which Ozma observes distant events at a set hour, and a room where Dorothy stays as a guest. The land also hosts courtly ceremony: at a grand procession, Princess Ozma placed her own coronet upon the winner of a race, proclaiming the Sawhorse "Prince of Horses" and declaring that hereafter all other horses in the Land of Oz must be considered imitations by comparison, before riding at the head of the procession back to the city.
