page.title: Princess Langwidere
page.content:
## Biography

Princess Langwidere once ruled the kingdom of Ev. She is the niece of Evoldo, whom she calls "a very wicked man," remarking that if he had drowned himself before selling his family, no one would have cared. Vain and languid, she cannot bear heat and refuses to join expeditions requiring it, declaring herself "heartily tired of ruling this stupid kingdom" and preferring leisure to admire her collection of heads. She keeps a mirrored chamber where she tries on her heads, including one with rich chestnut hair, dreamy walnut eyes, and a shapely hickorynut nose. Once relieved of her duties to the people of Ev, she was permitted by the Queen to keep her rooms and her cabinet of heads for as long as she lived.

## Relationships

**[[King]]** — family. The excerpts only hint at this tie; it is not stated outright.

**[[Ozma]]** — acquaintance. Their shared appearance seated opposite each other in the palace drawing-room suggests only a passing connection, nothing more.

**[[Queen of Ev]]** — other. Langwidere's relief from ruling seems linked to the Queen, who allowed her to keep her chamber and her cabinet of heads, though the excerpts do not spell out the nature of their bond.

page.title: Tiger
page.content:
## Biography

The Tiger is a striped, maneless companion who travels with Dorothy and the Cowardly Lion. He carries Dorothy on his back, who locks her arms around his striped neck for lack of a mane to cling to, and leaps clear between a giant iron guardian's legs to safety alongside the Lion and Ozma before its mallet strikes again. Addressed as "friend Tiger" by the Cowardly Lion, he agrees to face great danger with him to rescue a besieged army. Chronically hungry, he complains bitterly of being half-starved and begs to be allowed into the palace to become an ornament so he might no longer suffer the pangs of hunger. His appetite surfaces again when he eyes Billina greedily, remarking that her appearance "makes my mouth water," though he concedes it "wouldn't be right" to eat her. He also admits to being a little absent-minded at times.

## Relationships

**[[Cowardly Lion]]** — friend. The two seem close companions in danger, the Lion addressing him as "friend Tiger" before they cross the guarded threshold together.

**[[DOROTHY]]** — ally. Dorothy rides upon the Tiger's back, locking her arms around his striped neck during a perilous crossing, suggesting a bond of trust.

**[[BILLINA]]** — enemy. The Tiger eyes Billina greedily, remarking that her appearance "makes my mouth water" and clicking his jaws at her, which suggests a predatory antagonism he nonetheless restrains.

**[[Nome King]]** — acquaintance. Their connection appears only through shared presence within the expedition confronting him, suggesting no bond beyond that.

**[[Ozma]]** — friend. The Tiger addresses Ozma directly and promises to remember her words, suggesting a courteous rapport.

page.title: Evanna
page.content:
## Biography

Evanna is one of the five Princesses of Ev, a daughter of the Queen of Ev, named alongside her sisters Evrose, Evella, Evirene, and Evedna, and her brothers Evrob, Evington, Evardo, and Evroland. She was among the royal family transformed by the Nome King's enchantment into ornaments; she was freed when the yellow hen broke the spell binding one of the purple ornaments, revealing a sweet-faced girl whose golden hair fell in a cloud over her shoulders. The Queen of Ev recognized her at once, crying "Evanna! my own Evanna!" and clasped her to her bosom, covering her face with kisses.

page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Australia
- Place type: country
- Notable location: Sydney
- Status: non-fairy country

## Biography

Australia is a country outside the fairy lands, home to Uncle Henry, who lives in a pleasant room in Sydney. Unlike the Land of Oz or the Land of Ev, Australia has no magical properties of its own — the magic belt only works while its wearer remains in a fairy country, so a wish made with it would not carry its power to Australia once the destination was reached.

## Events

Dorothy uses Ozma's magic picture to look in on Uncle Henry, seeing him in Australia, sad and unwell, which leads her to decide she must return to him. She later says goodbye to her friends in Oz and is transported to Uncle Henry in Australia, where she comforts him as he recovers.

page.title: Chief Steward
page.content:
## Biography

The Chief Steward, also known as the Steward, attends the King's court and manages the reception of guests. When the King claps his hands to summon him after a guessing game leaves a visitor turned into an ornament, the Steward is ordered to show the newly arrived guests to their sleeping apartments. He leads Dorothy through a long hall to the first sleeping room, then settles the Scarecrow and Tiktok in the next room and the Lion and the Tiger in the third, before leaving them for the night. He wears a heavy gold chain around his neck as a mark of office, which seems to indicate that his post is held under the Nome King.

## Relationships

**[[Nome King]]** — employment. A gold chain worn by an enslaved ornament marked him as the Chief Steward of the Nome King, which could suggest some employment tie between a Chief Steward and the Nome King, though the connection is not stated outright.

page.title: Jim
page.content:
## Biography

Jim is a horse who pulls the buggy driven by Zeb, described by Zeb as an animal who "knows his business," though on the road to Hugson's Ranch he shows a stubborn streak, refusing to move until struck with the whip.

When invisible bears attack in the Valley of Voe, a magic leaf is rubbed on each of Jim's hoofs and on the buggy's tires, letting him walk on the surface of a river; he frees himself from his unseen attackers with a few kicks and escapes across the water, though not before deep gashes appear on his flanks.

Jim's Kentucky breeding is noted when he pounds along at a great rate despite an ungraceful gait. He loses a race against the Sawhorse, arriving panting at the canopy well after the wooden horse has already returned to cheers from the Ozites; the chapter that follows is one in which the Hungry Tiger teaches Jim a lesson.

According to the chapter orientation notes, Jim falls together with Dorothy, Zeb, and the buggy through a crack opened by an earthquake, landing in the glass city of the Mangaboos, where he and the kitten Eureka unexpectedly gain the power of speech.

## Narrative role

Jim is introduced as the horse pulling the buggy in which Zeb drives Dorothy from Hugson's Siding toward Hugson's Ranch, after Dorothy arrives there by train and meets Zeb. Shortly after, an earthquake splits the ground beneath them, and Jim falls with Dorothy, Zeb, and the buggy into a great crack leading deep underground. They land in the glass city of the Mangaboos, a vegetable people ruled by a Prince, where Jim unexpectedly gains the power of speech alongside the kitten Eureka. When the Mangaboos' new Princess later passes judgment on the group, she spares Dorothy, Zeb, and the Wizard but condemns Jim, along with Eureka and the piglets, to be driven into the Black Pit within the mountain. Jim, Dorothy, Zeb, Eureka, and the Wizard subsequently escape a group of invisible bears in the Valley of Voe by rubbing magic leaves onto their feet so they can walk on water. Once in Oz, Jim takes part in a reunion with Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, Billina, the Cowardly Lion, the Hungry Tiger, and the Woggle-Bug, an occasion that ends with a race between Jim and the Sawhorse. Jim loses that race and, in anger, kicks the Sawhorse hard enough to break its leg and ear, which prompts the Hungry Tiger to tackle him in response. Afterward, as Dorothy and Zeb bid farewell to Oz, Dorothy returns to Kansas while Zeb and Jim make their way back to Hugson's Ranch.

## Personality

Jim's early behavior marks him as stubborn: when urged onward at night he needed a shaken rein, a crack of the whip, and a touch to the flanks before he would move, answering with "a low moan of protest" rather than open refusal — reluctant compliance rather than defiance. Zeb's confidence in him ("Jim knows his business all right") suggests the horse is otherwise dependable once in motion.

That same underlying reliability surfaces under real danger: attacked by unseen assailants in the Valley of Voe, Jim frees himself with a few sharp kicks and obeys the Wizard's shouted order to run for the river without hesitation, suggesting an instinct for self-preservation paired with responsiveness to command in a crisis. His effort in the race against the Sawhorse — running hard despite lacking grace, "to do credit to his Kentucky breeding" — points to a competitive pride bound up with his lineage.

## Appearance

Jim is a horse of Kentucky breeding, a lineage reflected in his running style even though he does not look graceful while doing it. He has a long nose — patted by Zeb to calm him — and a big, boney build, with big hoofs that pound the ground at a great rate when he runs.

Eureka is noted nestling comfortably beside his big, boney body, underscoring his large frame relative to a small kitten.

## Powers

In the glass city of the Mangaboos, Jim unexpectedly gains the power of speech, a trait ordinary horses do not possess.

## Relationships

**[[Zeb]]** — acquaintance. Zeb is the one who unties, drives, and urges Jim throughout the journey, at one point coaxing him with "Jim knows his business all right—don't you, Jim?" while patting his nose; when Jim proves stubborn Zeb turns to the whip, after which Jim advances "with a low moan of protest." The bond between them seems to be one of routine familiarity between driver and horse rather than close companionship.

**[[Sawhorse]]** — friendly_rivalry. Racing the Sawhorse toward Ozma's canopy, Jim's "big hoofs pounded away at a great rate" in a manner said to do credit to his Kentucky breeding, yet the wooden Sawhorse proved "swifter than the wind" and reached the finish long before Jim came "panting up." The contest appears to have soured into real hostility, as Jim reportedly lashed out at the Sawhorse afterward — an episode remembered as the moment "the Hungry Tiger teaches Jim a lesson."

**[[DOROTHY]]** — friend. Dorothy rides in the buggy Jim pulls, including across the river in the Valley of Voe, where the horse carried the party safely once the magic leaves let him walk on the water's surface. Her question "Can your horse talk?" suggests a link to Jim's unexpected gain of speech, hinting at a bond of curiosity and trust rather than mere transport.

**[[Eureka]]** — friend. The kitten Eureka is described nestling "comfortably beside his big, boney body," a detail that could indicate an easy companionship between the two animals who, according to accounts of their descent into the underground realm, both unexpectedly gained the power of speech there.

**[[WIZARD]]** — ally. The Wizard directs Jim at critical moments, shouting "Run for the river!" so that the horse could free himself from unseen tormentors, and earlier rubbed the magic leaf upon Jim's hoofs to let him cross the water safely. Their interactions suggest the Wizard acts as a guide and protector to Jim rather than a mere companion in the buggy.

## Trivia

- Despite an ungainly gait, Jim's speed is credited to his Kentucky breeding.
- He is referred to as "the cab-horse," a term used to contrast him with the smaller, wooden Sawhorse.

page.title: Zeb
page.content:
## Biography

Zeb drives a buggy pulled by horse Jim, meeting Dorothy at Hugson's Siding and carrying her toward Hugson's Ranch when earthquake splits earth beneath them, plunging Zeb, Dorothy, Jim, and buggy underground into glass city of Mangaboos. Underground he travels alongside Dorothy, Wizard, Jim, and kitten Eureka through Valley of Voe, Pyramid Mountain, and Land of the Gargoyles.

In Valley of Voe, unseen bears attack the group; Zeb rubs magic leaf on his own feet and on Jim's hoofs and buggy tires so they can cross river without sinking, then runs across water to Dorothy after freeing Jim from the beasts. During race between Jim and Sawhorse, Jim kicks Sawhorse in anger and breaks its leg and ear; Zeb runs to Jim and warns him to control his temper or risk being torn apart by Hungry Tiger and Lion.

Zeb wants to return home. Seeing Hugson's Ranch in Ozma's enchanted picture makes him long for it, though he finds no one mourning him there; he tells Dorothy country of Oz is fine and he likes its people. When Dorothy uses Magic Belt to vanish and rejoin her aunt and uncle in Kansas, Zeb is bewildered by suddenness of her departure.

According to subjective chapter narration, Zeb, being boy, does not faint during fall underground, though badly frightened and clings tight to buggy seat expecting each moment his last.

## Personality

Zeb shows composure under acute physical danger: when the earth splits open beneath the buggy, he "did not faint, but ... was badly frightened, and clung to the buggy seat with a tight grip, expecting every moment would be his last" — fear registers, but it does not stop him from holding on.

His caution extends to others: after Jim's outburst against the Sawhorse, Zeb runs to the horse and warns him "that unless he controlled his temper in the future he would probably be torn to pieces," a watchfulness that suggests he weighs consequences the horse himself might not.

Faced with the unfamiliar, Zeb can be caught off guard rather than composed: Ozma's sudden departure with Dorothy leaves him "rather bewildered by the suddenness of it," pointing to an unease with abrupt, unexplained change.

He also holds an attachment to home tempered by openness to his surroundings: though he "wanted to see his home" and the sight of Hugson's Ranch made him "long to get back there," he tells Dorothy, "This is a fine country, and I like all the people that live in it" — the pull toward the familiar coexists with a genuine regard for the strange country he has come to know.

## Appearance

As Zeb descended with Dorothy toward the Glass City, illuminated by the five colored suns ringing its central globe, his face appeared blue and his hair pink under the shifting rainbow light cast by the suns.

## Relationships

**[[DOROTHY]]** — friend

**[[Jim]]** — acquaintance

**[[WIZARD]]** — ally

**[[Eureka]]** — acquaintance

**[[Princess Ozma]]** — budding_attraction

## Trivia

- As the buggy and its passengers descended toward the cluster of glowing colored spheres above the Glass City, the shifting light briefly turned Zeb's face blue and his hair pink.
- After the Sawhorse lost the race and Jim kicked it in anger, Zeb ran to Jim and privately warned him that unless he controlled his temper he would probably be torn to pieces.
- Looking at Ozma's enchanted picture of Hugson's Ranch, Zeb found that no one there seemed to be mourning his disappearance.

page.title: Eureka
page.content:
## Biography

Eureka is a small kitten belonging to Dorothy, who carries her along in a basket that a fellow traveler at first mistakes for a cage of canary-birds. Dorothy explains that she named the kitten Eureka because she found it, recalling that Uncle Henry says the word means "I have found it."

While the group crosses the river in the Valley of Voe using magic leaves that let them walk on water, Eureka is at first dreadfully afraid of getting wet, but soon frisks along beside the buggy without fear. During the crossing she snaps up and eats a small fish that swims too close to the surface, prompting Dorothy to caution her to be careful what she eats in the enchanted valley. Eureka is also able to speak, and when the group can hear one another again she admits that being able to see again makes her dreadfully hungry, asking the Wizard's permission to eat one of the fat little piglets.

Later, in the Princess's palace, Dorothy's white kitten is seen slipping out through a closed door and running up the stairs shortly before one of the Princess's tiny piglets goes missing. The Princess concludes that her piglet has been eaten and declares that the offender must be punished, but Dorothy protests that she does not believe Eureka would do such a dreadful thing. When Dorothy calls for her, Eureka is found hiding under the bed.

## Narrative role

Eureka is Dorothy's kitten, present when the group lands in the glass city of the Mangaboos, a vegetable people ruled by the Prince, where she and Jim unexpectedly gain the power of speech. The new Princess who takes power there spares Dorothy, [[Zeb]], and the Wizard, but condemns Jim, Eureka, and the piglets to be driven into the Black Pit within the mountain. Traveling on with the Wizard, Dorothy, Zeb, and Jim, Eureka escapes invisible bears in the Valley of Voe when the group rubs magic leaves on their feet to walk across the water.

Eureka later reveals a mismatch in a piglet's collar and confesses that the real piglet had fallen into a vase, where it is found alive. Ozma's white piglet then goes missing from her boudoir, and Dorothy's kitten Eureka is seen fleeing the room. Ozma accuses Eureka of the piglet's disappearance and orders her imprisoned and put on trial for murder before a jury of nine. Before the verdict, the Wizard secretly gives Tin Woodman a duplicate piglet to produce as proof of Eureka's innocence should she be convicted. The jury ultimately finds Eureka guilty, but Tin Woodman produces the duplicate piglet, seemingly proving her innocence.

## Personality

Eureka's most consistent trait is her appetite: confronted with easy prey — a fish in the river, the Wizard's tiny piglets — her first instinct is to eat it, and she voices this desire openly, at one point asking outright whether she may "eat just one of the fat little piglets." Hunger, for her, arrives together with the pleasure of simply being able to see again, suggesting a direct, unreflective link between appetite and satisfaction.

She is also adaptable and quick to recover from fear. Crossing the river in the Valley of Voe, she is at first "dreadfully afraid of getting wet," but once set down she abandons that fear entirely and trots alongside the buggy "without being scared a bit." This rapid shift from anxiety to playful ease suggests a kitten who, once a threat has passed, does not dwell on it.

Her boldness draws suspicion from others. When Princess Ozma's piglet disappears and the kitten is seen fleeing the scene, the household immediately assumes Eureka is guilty — a conclusion Dorothy, defending her, refuses to accept. Whatever the truth of that particular incident, the readiness of others to suspect her matches an earlier description of her as not always "well behaved."

## Appearance

Eureka is a white kitten kept by Dorothy, who carries her rather than a cage when traveling.

## Powers

Eureka's defining trait is an unexplained capacity for speech, unusual for a cat. During the crossing of the Valley of Voe she addresses the Wizard directly, telling him she can see again and asking, "Mr. Wizard, may I eat just one of the fat little piglets?" Beyond this ability to speak and reason, Eureka shows an ordinary hunting reflex, snatching a fish from the water and eating it "as quick as a wink" when the party crosses the enchanted river.

## Relationships

**[[DOROTHY]]** — friend. Eureka is Dorothy's own kitten, carried in her arms across the enchanted river and called back anxiously ("Come back, Eureka!" she called, in distress) and defended by her when accused of eating the Princess's piglet.

**[[Jim]]** — friend. The two seem to share an easy companionship, Eureka "nestling comfortably beside his big, boney body."

**[[WIZARD]]** — acquaintance. Their acquaintance appears bound up with the Wizard's own admission to "friends" that "the thing was only a trick," suggesting Eureka was present for such confidences.

**[[Zeb]]** — acquaintance. Zeb's recollection of the "first time I ever saw a pink cat" suggests a memorable early encounter between the two.

**[[Billina]]** — enemy. Eureka appears to have "leaped up with a sharp claw fiercely bared to strike Billina a blow," suggesting hostility between them.

## Trivia

- The name "Eureka" comes from the exclamation meaning "I have found it"; Dorothy named her kitten this way, explaining that Uncle Henry had taught her the meaning of the word.
- Eureka is Dorothy's white kitten; when Zeb first heard her meowing and asked if it were canary-birds, Dorothy corrected him that it was only Eureka.
- While crossing the enchanted river in the Valley of Voe, Eureka was at first dreadfully afraid of getting wet but soon moved confidently alongside the buggy, catching and eating a small fish that swam too near the surface.

page.title: Sorcerer
page.content:
## Biography

The Sorcerer, also known as Gwig, is a practitioner of sorcery among the Mangaboo people, summoned before them with the call "Come to us, oh, Gwig!" He identifies himself directly, stating "My name is Gwig," while turning his heartless, cruel eyes upon a rival and daring him to equal the sorcery he is about to perform. Displaying sorcery in this manner is described as one of the things Gwig usually did to prove he was a sorcerer, though the Mangaboo people listening show no great interest in the demonstration.

## Relationships

**[[WIZARD]]** — enemy. Their rivalry surfaces in dueling boasts of sorcery — Gwig declaring "I'll beat Old Prickly, all right" and demanding "Let me see you equal the sorcery I am about to perform" — which seems to place him in direct competition with the Wizard.

**[[Prince]]** — employment. Gwig tells the Prince, "Quite sure, my Prince. My sorcery tells me so," which suggests he serves the Prince's court in some advisory capacity.

**[[DOROTHY]]** — enemy. He is described as having looked toward the little girl with cold, cruel eyes, which could indicate hostility toward her.

## Biography

Hugson's Ranch is a rural homestead reached by buggy along a well-known road leading up to its gates. It is the home of Uncle Hugson, who comes out to greet arrivals in astonishment, and of Zeb, who considers it home and speaks fondly of the country and its people. Dorothy's Uncle Henry also travels there for a visit after reaching San Francisco, suggesting the ranch serves as a destination for family arriving from farther afield, reached by train to a nearby siding and then by buggy.

## Events

At the ranch, Dorothy Gale arrives by train at Hugson's Siding and is met by Zeb, who drives her there in a buggy pulled by the horse Jim. Later, after parting ways with Dorothy, Zeb and Jim return to the ranch.

## Biography

L. Frank Baum is credited on the title page as writer of the account, alongside illustrator John R. Neill. The dedication names Harriet A. B. Neal. In a preface addressed to readers, Baum acknowledges that "the books are partly yours," crediting readers' suggestions for guiding the telling of the stories and calling their assistance "clever and thoughtful."

page.title: Uncle Hugson
page.content:
## Biography

Uncle Hugson is the owner of Hugson's Ranch. When a horse-drawn buggy reaches the ranch gates, he comes out himself, standing with uplifted arms and wide open mouth, staring in amazement at the arrival. He is said to have been having "a fine visit" with another visitor. One character remarks that laboring for him amounts to "a great deal," a claim answered with the retort that the speaker is "a splendid worker" — suggesting Hugson expects diligent work from those in his employ.

## Biography

Pyramid Mountain lies beyond a stretch of the valley, reached by following the river that flows in its direction. To get there, travelers must cross a mile or so of the valley, a stretch with few houses, orchards, or flowers, where the risk of encountering savage bears is feared. A man with braids maintains a factory halfway up the mountain, in a spot he describes as no longer inhabited by him at the surface, having lived there for many years.

## Events

After resisting the invisibility-granting dama-fruit and learning they must cross toward Pyramid Mountain to continue their journey, the travelers make their way there by river. Once at the mountain, they climb a long spiral stairway inside it leading toward the Land of the Gargoyles.

page.title: Hungry Tiger
page.content:
## Biography

The Hungry Tiger is a resident of Oz and a friend of the Cowardly Lion. Introduced by the Sawhorse as "the terror of the jungle, who longs to devour fat babies but is prevented by his conscience from doing so," he is known among the folk of Oz for this constant inner struggle between appetite and restraint. His standing in Oz is such that even Eureka, suspected of trying to eat Ozma's piglet, found herself shunned by him along with the rest of the palace.

## Relationships

**[[Jim]]** — friendly_rivalry. Their interactions suggest a lighthearted rivalry rather than true hostility.

**[[DOROTHY]]** — friend. Their association suggests a friendly acquaintance among Oz's residents.

**[[Eureka]]** — enemy. Their distance suggests strained relations, as the Hungry Tiger reportedly preferred not to associate with her after the piglet incident.

**[[Sawhorse]]** — friend. Their shared appearance among Oz's companions suggests a cordial bond.

page.title: Omaha
page.content:
## Biography

Omaha is the birthplace of the Wizard, whose father, a politician, gave him the elaborate name Oscar Zoroaster Phadrig Isaac Norman Henkle Emmannuel Ambroise Diggs. After his balloon escaped too soon during his first departure with Dorothy, he was carried back alone to Omaha, where he found that all his old friends were dead or had moved away. With nothing else to do, he rejoined a circus there and resumed making balloon ascensions until an earthquake caught him. He also refers to a local expression, "as we say in Omaha," when describing how he directed the building of his domain.

page.title: Valley of Voe
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Valley of Voe
- Also known as: Voe
- Place type: Valley
- Status: Inhabited

## Biography

The Valley of Voe, also known as Voe, is a valley reached through a tunnel in a glass mountain. It is inhabited by the people of Voe, who are invisible — when asked "are you all invisible?", a woman of Voe answers "Surely" and adds, with a low, rippling laugh, "Are you surprised that you are unable to see the people of Voe?" The valley holds pretty cottages along a broad stream, with fruits and flowers growing plentifully, including cherries, plums, and a fruit called damas that the people of Voe are fond of. Dangerous bears, themselves unseen, live near the orchards of the valley.

## Appearance

From a landing reached partway up the stairs leading out of the valley, a rift in the mountainside opens onto a view of the Valley of Voe lying far below, its cottages appearing like toy houses at that distance. The stairway itself is broad and low, wide enough for a horse to draw a buggy up it.

## Events

A group fleeing through a tunnel in a glass mountain emerges into the invisible Valley of Voe, where unseen inhabitants warn them of dangerous invisible bears nearby. To escape the bears, the people of Voe's secret is used: rubbing certain leaves on the soles of the feet allows a person to walk on water without sinking, a method the people of Voe rely on themselves to travel and evade enemies. The group crosses water this way before climbing the mountain stairway to leave the valley.

## Trivia

- The leaf-rubbing method of walking on water is described as a secret the bears themselves do not know.
- The valley's stairway is broad and low enough for a horse harnessed to a buggy to climb it.

- Aliases: Mangaboo, MANGABOOS, Mangaboos

## Biography

The Land of the Mangaboos lies beneath six colored suns and is home to the Mangaboo people, ruled by a vegetable Princess. When Dorothy, Zeb, and the Wizard arrived there, the Princess and a throng of her people met them at the House of the Sorcerer. After consulting her advisors, the Princess declared that the newcomers, whom she called "meat people," did not belong in the Land of the Mangaboos and could not remain there — and that since they could not simply go away, they must be destroyed.

infobox_fields.friends_allies: [[Dorothy]], [[Polly]], [[Jack Pumpkinhead]], [[King Bud of Noland]], [[Nick Chopper]], [[Ozma]], [[Santa Claus]], [[Tik-tok]]

page.content:
## Biography

Button-Bright travels with a group that becomes stranded at the edge of the Deadly Desert, unable to reach the Land of Oz. When the shaggy man asks what to do next, having ruled out going ahead or turning back, Button-Bright answers only "Don't know." Left to occupy himself while the others sit in thought, he takes a stick and digs in the earth. Asked to join in dancing, he declines, saying he doesn't want to dance, and instead sits down wearily upon the soft grass.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. Their bond seems suggested by an episode in which Polly and Dorothy tried to comfort Button-Bright, and by their shared confusion when stranded at the edge of the Deadly Desert, where Button-Bright answered "Don't know" and Dorothy added, just as uncertainly, "I'm sure I don't know, either."

**[[Polly]]** — friend. The same episode, in which Polly and Dorothy tried to comfort Button-Bright, suggests a friendly bond — notably after Button-Bright sat down wearily on the grass and declared he did not want to dance.

**[[Scarecrow]]** — acquaintance. Button-Bright is described as wonderfully attracted by the straw man, which could indicate a friendly acquaintance between them.

**[[THE shaggy man]]** — acquaintance. Their exchanges while stranded at the edge of the desert, where the shaggy man addressed the group Button-Bright belonged to in deciding what to do next, suggest an acquaintance between them.

**[[Jack Pumpkinhead]]** — friend. A friendly bond is suggested, though no direct exchange between the two appears among the available passages.

page.title: Polly
page.content:
## Biography

Polly travels with Dorothy, Button-Bright, and the shaggy man on the road toward Oz. Dorothy addresses her as the Rainbow's Daughter and asks whether she can work magic, but Polly answers plainly, "No, dear," even after Dorothy suggests she ought to know some, given that heritage. Dorothy speaks warmly of her, thanking her for an offer to dance upon the rainbows they encounter, though Dorothy declines, worried the rainbows would prove soft and squnshy underfoot. When Johnny Dooit rigs a sail from rope and canvas, Polly watches the work take shape with the same absorbed interest as Button-Bright.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. Dorothy thanks her warmly on the rainbow — "It's very good of you, Polly" — suggesting an easy, friendly rapport between them.

**[[Button-Bright]]** — friend. Polly sits with Button-Bright and Dorothy on the rainbow and later watches Johnny Dooit's sail-rigging alongside him, both "absorbed in the same interest," hinting at a comfortable companionship.

**[[Nick Chopper]]** — friend. Their tie appears only faintly, tied to a shared moment of delight within the traveling group.

**[[Scarecrow]]** — acquaintance. The connection seems limited to shared company among the travelers, with no direct exchange recorded.

**[[Tik-tok]]** — acquaintance. Polly's link to Tik-tok seems slight, likely no more than co-presence within the group.

page.title: Polychrome
page.content:
## Biography

Polychrome is known as the Rainbow's Daughter, one of those who live upon the rainbow among the fleecy clouds. When Dorothy, addressing her as "Polly," asks whether she can perform any magic, Polychrome answers plainly that she cannot, explaining that those who dwell on the rainbow have no use for magic.

During a crossing by boat, Polychrome clings to the bow, watching ahead until she makes out a row of jagged rocks marking the edge of a desert, beyond which lies a tableland of green grass and trees. According to the account of this crossing, she travels alongside Dorothy, the shaggy man, Button-Bright, and Toto, stranded at the edge of the Deadly Desert until a sand-boat is built to carry them across; the boat eventually strikes the rocks at the desert's far edge, though the party lands unharmed in the yellow Country of the Winkies.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. Dorothy calls her "Polly" and asks whether she knows any magic, to which Polychrome answers plainly that she does not.
**[[Jellia Jamb]]** — acquaintance. Jellia Jamb personally ushers the Rainbow's Daughter to her apartments, suggesting Polychrome receives particular attention.
**[[Ozma]]** — friend. Ozma reportedly rises to greet the Rainbow's Daughter in her sweetest and most cordial manner, which could suggest a warm bond between them.
**[[Santa Claus]]** — friend. Their meeting seems to suggest a friendly acquaintance, though the excerpts give no further detail.
**[[THE shaggy man]]** — friend. Their bond appears friendly, though the excerpts do not detail its nature further.

page.title: Johnny Dooit
page.content:
## Biography

Johnny Dooit is a small man summoned by the shaggy man through the power of the Love Magnet, called with the words "Dear Johnny Dooit, come to me. I need you bad as bad can be." When Dorothy asks what he can do, the shaggy man answers "Anything," with confidence. Johnny Dooit has a broad nose that sticks up a little and eyes that are twinkling and merry; his hands and arms are as hard and tough as the leather of the apron he wears, giving Dorothy the impression that he has done a great deal of hard work in his lifetime. According to the account of that day, once summoned he quickly builds a sand-boat to carry the shaggy man, Dorothy, and their companions across the Deadly Desert; the boat crashes into rocks at the desert's far edge, though the travelers land unharmed in the Country of the Winkies.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — acquaintance. Johnny Dooit seems to have been introduced to Dorothy by the shaggy man.

**[[THE shaggy man]]** — friend. Their bond appears tied to the Love Magnet, which the shaggy man describes as drawing to him "a powerful friend."

**[[Princess]]** — acquaintance. Johnny Dooit appears to have thanked the Princess for her hospitality.

page.title: Santa Claus
page.content:
## Biography

Santa Claus is a rotund, rosy-faced figure with laughing eyes and a bushy beard as white as snow. He greets a gathered group warmly, crying out his delight at seeing them and trotting briskly up a long room toward them. He recognizes Button-Bright at once, holding the boy up to kiss him and remarking on how far he is from home. He also leans over to whisper something to the Wizard, who smiles and nods as though he understands. Turning his attention to Polychrome, the Rainbow's Daughter, Santa Claus approaches her and observes, admiringly, that she seems even farther from home than any of the others present.

## Relationships

**[[Ozma]]** — friend. Ozma's invitation seems to be what brought Santa Claus to the gathering, suggesting a friendly bond between them, though the excerpts do not detail its origin further.

**[[Button-Bright]]** — friend. Santa Claus greets him warmly, exclaiming "And here's Button-Bright, I declare!" and holding him up to kiss him, indicating an established, affectionate familiarity.

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. Dorothy recognizes Santa Claus at once and eagerly asks whether he also knows Button-Bright, suggesting a friendly rapport between them, though its nature is not elaborated on.

**[[Polychrome]]** — friend. Santa Claus notices her among those present and trots over to her, observing admiringly that "the Rainbow's Daughter is farther from home than any of you," which suggests a warm, attentive regard.

**[[Wizard]]** — friend. He leans over to whisper something in the Wizard's ear, and the Wizard smiles and nods as if understanding him, suggesting an easy familiarity between the two.

page.title: TWINKLE
page.content:
## Biography

Twinkle is a little girl at the center of several separate adventures. In one, she captures a mud turtle that turns out to be a fairy prince. In another, she is taken underground to visit Mr. Woodchuck's family and neighbors, where she discovers what they think of traps and of the people who set them. Twinkle also keeps a pet, Jim Crow, who later escapes and becomes a robber among the birds.

page.title: High Chamberlain
page.content:
## Biography

The High Chamberlain serves at the palace, with duties centered on receiving and announcing visitors to the Throne-Room. During festivities held there, the High Chamberlain threw open the doors of the Throne-Room to admit arriving guests, among them a gingerbread man. After King John Dough presented Ozma with a birthday gift, the High Chamberlain escorted the visitors from Hiland and Loland to their rooms, then hurried back to receive further arrivals in a most official manner, again announcing entrants such as a band of Ryls from the Happy Valley. The role seems to place the High Chamberlain in Ozma's service, hurrying forward to announce arriving names on her behalf.

## Relationships

**[[Ozma]]** — employment. The High Chamberlain seems to serve in Ozma's court, as suggested by the moment he "hurried forward to announce the names" of arriving visitors.

page.title: John Dough
page.content:
## Biography

John Dough is a figure of rank who attends a great banquet hosted by Princess Ozma, where he is given a golden throne to sit in alongside Queen Zixi, King Bud, the Queen of Ev and her son Evardo, and the Queen of Merryland — a mark of his standing among the assembled dignitaries. He is accompanied by his own retinue: a Head Booleywag, who quickly becomes a favorite among the other guests, and a group of Hilanders and Lolanders, who are seated together at a table reserved for the visiting attendants and soldiers of the various guests.

## Relationships

**[[Scarecrow]]** — acquaintance

page.title: Dyna
page.content:
## Biography

Dyna is an old woman living in the Emerald City. She is a relative of the crooked Sorcerer who invented the magic Powder of Life; when the Sorcerer fell down a precipice and was killed, all his possessions passed to her. Dyna traveled to the mountains where the Sorcerer had lived and took away everything she considered of value, including a small bottle of the Powder of Life — though she did not know it was magic.

Dyna once kept a large blue bear as a pet, until it choked to death on a fishbone. She loved the bear so dearly that she made a rug from its skin, leaving the head and four paws on the hide, and kept the rug on the floor of her front parlor.

page.title: Deadly Desert
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Deadly Desert
- Type: Desert
- Location: Separates the Land of Oz from the Kingdom of Ev, lying to the north of Oz

## Biography

The Deadly Desert is a vast expanse of sand that separates the Land of Oz from the Kingdom of Ev, which lies just across it to the north. Crossing it is perilous: a sand-boat carrying the shaggy man and his companions was pushed to great speed by a raised sail, moving so fast that everyone aboard had to hold fast to the sides and scarcely dared breathe. Ozma, watching the travelers' progress the whole way in her Magic Picture, stated that she twice considered using the Magic Belt to save them and transport them to the Emerald City — once when the Scoodlers caught them, and again when they reached the Deadly Desert itself. On both occasions the shaggy man was able to help the group out without her intervention.

## Events

Dorothy, the shaggy man, Button-Bright, Toto, and Polychrome became stranded at the edge of the Deadly Desert, with no way to reach the Land of Oz.

## Physical

The sand of the desert lies in billows and is very uneven in places, causing a boat crossing it to rock dangerously from side to side. Despite the unevenness of the terrain, a sand-boat driven by a raised sail could cross it without tipping over, reaching a speed great enough to frighten even the shaggy man, who wondered how to make the craft go slower.

## Trivia

- Ozma nearly used her Magic Belt to rescue the travelers from the desert, just as she had earlier considered doing when the Scoodlers caught them.
- The shaggy man was credited with helping the group out of danger both times, without need for Ozma's intervention.

## References

<references/>

page.title: Royal Palace
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Royal Palace
- Type: Palace
- Location: Emerald City
- Status: Inhabited

## Biography

The Royal Palace is a vast, noble, and elegant building so distinctive that it can be recognized on sight. Its gardens and grounds are enclosed by a separate wall, one that is lower and thinner than the wall surrounding the Emerald City itself but more daintily designed, and built entirely of green marble. Visitors are received in a grand hall upon entering. Several residents keep permanent quarters there: Tik-Tok lives at the Royal Palace, the Tin Woodman is given the same room each time he visits Ozma, and Dorothy keeps a suite of rooms that she occupies whenever she is in the Emerald City. According to Dorothy, all of her friends are welcome at Ozma's palace.

## Appearance

The palace grounds are set apart by their own boundary wall, distinct from the wall around the City. This inner wall is described as more daintily designed than the City wall, though not as high or thick, and it is built entirely of green marble.

## Events

Ozma's golden chariot, escorted by the Cowardly Lion and the Hungry Tiger, meets an arriving party and brings them through the Emerald City into the Royal Palace, where they are received in the grand hall.

## Trivia

- The servants of the Royal Palace marched together as their own group during a public procession, positioned ahead of the general crowd.

## References

<references/>

page.title: THE shaggy man
page.content:
## Biography

The shaggy man is a wanderer marked by his shaggy attire — a shaggy hat, and later shaggy creamy stockings of silk and shaggy slippers of rose leather with ruby buckles. Upon being brought as a guest into a great hall of a fine palace, he stood holding his shaggy hat, uncertain what would become of him, reflecting that he had perhaps never before been a guest anywhere. Finding himself unexpectedly surrounded by luxury — a bath edged with emeralds as large as door-knobs and water clear as crystal — he gazed upon it all in silent amazement before deciding, in his own wise way, to take advantage of his good fortune.

After dressing in his new finery, the shaggy man admired himself at length in a long mirror. He then discovered a mother-of-pearl chest decorated with silver vines and clustered rubies, engraved with the words "THE SHAGGY MAN: HIS BOX OF ORNAMENTS." Opening the unlocked chest, he found it filled with rich jewels, from which he took a fine golden watch with a large chain, several handsome finger-rings, and a ruby ornament to pin upon the breast of his shaggy shirt-bosom.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. Their bond seems to grow through shared circumstance: it is with Dorothy that he reads aloud the desert's warning sign, and together they conclude "we mustn't try it," suggesting a companionship formed along the road.

**[[Nick Chopper]]** — friend. Nick Chopper reportedly "already... loved the shaggy man," hinting at a warm regard forming between them even before the shaggy man's ownership of the Love Magnet became known.

**[[Button-Bright]]** — acquaintance. The shaggy man is described pulling Button-Bright out of a hole, suggesting a protective, if casual, acquaintance between the two.

**[[Johnny Dooit]]** — friend. He calls on Johnny Dooit by name through the Love Magnet — "Dear Johnny Dooit, come to me. I need you bad as bad can be" — and answers "Anything" with confidence when asked what Johnny can do, suggesting a trusting friendship.

**[[Ozma]]** — acquaintance. His question, "But I thought Princess Ozma ruled Oz," suggests an awareness of her rule more befitting an acquaintance with her reputation than someone close to her.

page.title: Shaggy Man
page.content:
## Biography

The Shaggy Man travels in the company of Dorothy, the Wizard, Uncle Henry, and Omby Amby. In conversation with the Wizard, he asks about the Fuddles, said to be among the most peculiar people in the Land of Oz, though the Wizard admits he does not know in what way. During a search involving a lost item, he first guesses that a distressed woman has lost her mirror, and is corrected; he later cries out that he has found a queer-shaped piece with a mouth on it, though when tried against an eye and nose the parts do not match.

When a cry for help goes up, the Shaggy Man jumps from the wagon together with the Wizard, Uncle Henry, and Omby Amby to go to a man's assistance, with Dorothy following behind. On another occasion he questions a woman sobbing over the thought that she might have pricked her foot, and elsewhere asks who designed the mansion built for a farmer who wished for land of his own, learning that Jack Pumpkinhead, himself a farmer, had done so.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — friend. When a lost piece turns up, the Shaggy Man cries "I've found it!" and runs to Dorothy with it, suggesting a helpful, friendly rapport between them.

**[[Wizard]]** — acquaintance. The two converse familiarly, as when the Shaggy Man asks "In what way?" in reply to the Wizard's remark about the Fuddles, suggesting an easy, conversational acquaintance.

**[[Ozma]]** — friend. Evidence is slight, but a line where the Shaggy Man declares "And so will I" alongside her seems to suggest a friendly bond.

**[[Roquat]]** — acquaintance. Evidence for this connection is minimal, and the nature of the acquaintance remains unclear.

## References

<references/>

page.title: King Dox
page.content:
## Biography

King Dox rules Foxville; the excerpts note his full title as King Renard of Foxville, though he prefers to be called King Dox. Dorothy asked Ozma to invite him, along with King Kik-a-bray of Dunkiton, to Ozma's birthday celebration, and Ozma confirmed the invitations had already been sent. He arrived at the Throne-Room magnificently dressed in a new feather costume, wearing white kid mittens over his paws, a flower in his buttonhole, and his hair parted in the middle. He thanked Dorothy fervently for securing his invitation, having longed all his life to visit Oz, and strutted rather absurdly as he was introduced to the assembled guests. On learning that Dorothy was a Princess of Oz, he insisted on kneeling at her feet before retiring backward — a maneuver considered dangerous, since he might have stubbed his paw and fallen.

## Relationships

King Dox, also called King Renard, rules Foxville. He arrives at Ozma's birthday party in a feather costume, white kid mittens, a flower in his button-hole, and hair parted in the middle. He thanks Dorothy for securing his invitation to Oz, a place he had long wished to visit, and kneels at her feet upon learning she is a Princess of Oz.

page.title: Musicker
page.content:
## Biography

The Musicker is a performer known for producing music considered too noisy to be enjoyed in company. Princess Ozma declines to invite him to her celebration, explaining that when music is not very good and is indulged in constantly, it is better that the performer remain alone. Button-Bright, however, declares that he likes the Musicker's music, a view Dorothy does not share.

page.title: King Bud of Noland
page.content:
## Biography

King Bud of Noland, also known as King Bud, rules the kingdom of Noland, whose borders adjoin those of Ix. He travels with his sister, the Princess Fluff, described as dainty and fair-haired, to attend the birthday celebration of Ozma of Oz, a journey undertaken because he and Queen Zixi of Ix are friends and their neighboring kingdoms allowed them to travel together from their distant domains.

At the birthday gathering, King Bud is announced with full royal honors, styled "His Serene and Tremendous Majesty," alongside Queen Zixi of Ix and the Princess Fluff. He and his sister bring splendid gifts for Ozma, adding to a table already heavy with presents from other visiting dignitaries.

During the grand procession honoring Ozma, King Bud of Noland and the Princess Fluff march together, positioned among a long line of notable figures that includes Queen Zixi of Ix, John Dough, the Cherub, the Queen of Merryland, the Queen of Ev and her royal children, the Braided Man, the Candy Man, King Dox of Foxville, King Kik-a-bray of Dunkiton, and Johnny Dooit. The crowd cheers this procession as heartily as those who came before.

## Personality

King Bud of Noland is sparsely characterized within these excerpts, but two details suggest his disposition. He travels from his own domain together with Queen Zixi of Ix specifically to honor Ozma of Oz on her birthday, an action that points to a courteous and respectful nature toward fellow rulers. He and his sister, the Princess Fluff, also bring "many splendid gifts" to the celebration, a generosity that reinforces the impression of a considerate, sociable monarch who values maintaining friendly ties with allied kingdoms.

## Relationships

**[[Princess]]** — family. Text names him traveling with "his sister, the Princess Fluff," suggesting close kinship tied to their joint journey honoring Ozma.

**[[Button-Bright]]** — friend. Bond seems warm and quick — Button-Bright reportedly "accepted him as a chum at once and did not want him to go away."

## Trivia

- Announced at court with the formal title "His Serene and Tremendous Majesty, King Bud of Noland," alongside Queen Zixi of Ix ("Her Sublime and Resplendent Majesty") and his sister, Princess Fluff ("Her Royal Highness").
- Noland borders the kingdom of Ix, which is why King Bud and Princess Fluff traveled together with Queen Zixi to Ozma's birthday celebration.
- Brought splendid gifts for Ozma of Oz, added to a table already loaded with presents from other guests.
- In the birthday procession, King Bud and Princess Fluff marched directly behind the Queen of Merryland and her wooden soldiers, and just ahead of the Queen of Ev and her ten royal children.

## References

* [[Button-Bright]] — Friend (ch.1)<ref>The Road to Oz, chapter 1</ref>

page.title: Omby Amby
page.content:
## Biography

Omby Amby is a companion on a journey through the Land of Oz, traveling alongside Dorothy, Uncle Henry, the Wizard, and the Shaggy Man. During a puzzle-solving episode, he proves observant and helpful, discovering scattered pieces — including a hand holding a knitting needle and, later, a mouth — that others use to reassemble figures such as old Larry and Grandmother Gnit. He is knowledgeable about the geography and customs of Oz, explaining to the group that Flutterbudget Center and Rigmarole Town are known as "the Defensive Settlements of Oz."

When a cry for help is heard, Omby Amby joins the Wizard, Uncle Henry, and the Shaggy Man in leaping from the wagon to come to a stranger's aid. In an exchange with a man afraid to sleep for fear his eyes might grow shut, Omby Amby responds with plain, direct questioning, asking why the man cannot sleep and whether he had ever heard of such a thing happening.

## Relationships

**[[Ozma]]** — employment. An account suggests Ozma sent Omby Amby to the palace for the Magic Belt, though the excerpts do not confirm this as settled fact.

**[[Tiktok]]** — acquaintance. Omby Amby addresses Tiktok directly, asking why his "clock-work brains" interrupt the group's enjoyment, which points to a passing familiarity between the two rather than any deeper stated bond.

**[[Wizard]]** — ally. When a man's cries for help rang out, Omby Amby jumped from the wagon together with the Wizard, Uncle Henry, and the Shaggy Man to come to his assistance, suggesting the two acted in concert on that occasion.

## References

page.title: BUNNYBURY
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Bunnybury

## Biography

Bunnybury is reached by a road branching off near a signpost marked with two signs, one reading "TAKE THE OTHER ROAD TO BUNBURY" and the other "TAKE THE OTHER ROAD TO BUNNYBURY," set upon a large oak where the path splits and disappears into the trees in both directions. The road leading to Bunnybury is a narrow strip, worn hard and smooth, but not wide enough for Dorothy's feet to tread. Strangers arriving there were welcomed upon entry.

## Events

Dorothy later recounts her day's adventures to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, describing her visits to Utensia, Bunbury, and Bunnybury.

## References

page.title: FUDDLECUMJIG
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Fuddlecumjig
- Region: Land of Oz

## Biography

Fuddlecumjig is a destination within the Land of Oz, reached by a road marked with a sign-post reading "THIS WAY TO FUDDLECUMJIG." It is known as the home of the Fuddles, described as the most peculiar people in all the Land of Oz. Ozma is said to have thought that visitors might enjoy the Fuddles, prompting a detour to the place.

## References

<references/>

page.title: Bunbury
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Bunbury
- Place type: settlement of cracker houses

## Biography

Bunbury is reached by a little-traveled path that runs in a zigzag course through the trees, eventually opening onto a clearing filled with the queerest houses to be found anywhere. The houses are built entirely of crackers laid out in tiny squares, taking many pretty and ornamental shapes, with balconies and porches supported by posts of bread-sticks and roofs shingled with wafer-crackers.

Dorothy chose the path toward Bunbury after seeing signs pointing the way, reasoning that "Bunbury sounds like something to eat." She and the Yellow Hen followed the path together while wandering hungry through the woods, hoping to find some sign of civilization.

## Events

Dorothy later recounts her day's adventures to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, describing among them her visit to Bunbury alongside her visits to Utensia and Bunnybury.

## References

<references/>

page.title: Fuddles
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Fuddles
- Region: Near Fuddlecumjig, Land of Oz

## Biography

Fuddles is a name given both to a people and to the territory they occupy, lying about two miles beyond Fuddlecumjig in the Land of Oz. The region is reached by the main road that passes through pleasant farming country. The Fuddles are said to be the most peculiar people in all the Land of Oz, though the exact nature of their peculiarity is not detailed. Grandmother Gnit, a maker of mittens, is counted among the Fuddles, suggesting the inhabitants of this area practice crafts such as knitting.

## References

<references/>

page.title: Utensia
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Utensia
- Place type: Kingdom
- Ruler: King Kleaver

## Biography

Utensia is a kingdom ruled by King Kleaver, inhabited by sentient household utensils; a spoon among its subjects addressed Dorothy directly, retorting that the inhabitants have never heard of Ozma of Oz and are not her subjects. Dorothy had never heard of Utensia before her visit, and she supposed that Ozma likewise had no knowledge of it.

Some manner of threat was made toward Dorothy during her time there, though it did not trouble her — she did not believe herself to be in any danger, and treated the encounter as a new and interesting adventure, agreeing to be taken into Utensia to see what King Kleaver's kingdom was like.

## Events

Dorothy later recounts her visit to Utensia — along with her visits to Bunbury and Bunnybury — to Aunt Em and Uncle Henry.

## References

<references/>

page.title: Grand Gallipoot
page.content:
## Biography

The Grand Gallipoot rules the Growleywogs and stands beside the Chief of the Whimsies before the Nome King, flanked by skillful generals as part of an allied force. Fierce and powerful in bearing, the Grand Gallipoot's presence unsettles even the Nome King and General Guph. Eager to move against the Emerald City, the Grand Gallipoot asks the Nome King how long the march will take and is told that starting at midnight would bring them there by daybreak. When a captive is discussed, the Grand Gallipoot angrily insists on claiming her as a personal slave, prompting King Roquat to hastily put off the matter.

page.title: Keeper of the Wicket
page.content:
## Biography

The Keeper of the Wicket, also known as Bristle, is an official among the rabbit people encountered by Dorothy. His dress is described as rich, though it is noted as commonplace when set against the more splendid silk-and-satin costumes worn by the other rabbit folk around him. In this capacity he acts as herald: it is he who, in a pompous voice, calls out for the crowd to make way for Princess Dorothy as she arrives from Ozma of Oz, and who later commands the line of rabbit soldiers before the palace entrance to salute her. His exchange with the King, in which he inquires whether His Majesty is at leisure, suggests his position places him in service to the King.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — acquaintance. The Keeper of the Wicket personally announced Dorothy's arrival and called for her salute both at the city gates and at the palace, a formal reception that seems to reflect the regard owed a visiting dignitary rather than a personal bond.

**[[King]]** — employment. The Keeper of the Wicket inquired whether the King was at leisure, which suggests a position of service or subordination within the King's court.

## References

<references/>

page.title: Grandmother Gnit
page.content:
## Biography

Grandmother Gnit is one of the Fuddles, a people living about two miles beyond Fuddlecumjig who must be pieced together like a puzzle to take physical shape. She once made a pair of mittens, and one of the Fuddles claims to know her well enough to identify every piece belonging to her. When Omby Amby found a hand holding a knitting needle, the travelers decided to put Grandmother Gnit together; she proved an easier puzzle than old Larry, and once assembled she turned out to be a pleasant old lady who welcomed them cordially.

status.quote: Grandmother Gnit made me the mittens, and she's one of the Fuddles.
Grandmother Gnit made me the mittens, and she's one of the Fuddles.

page.title: Mr. Bunn
page.content:
## Biography

Mr. Bunn is a resident of Bunbury, a town built entirely of bread and baked goods. He speaks stiffly in defense of his town's identity, telling visitors, "I admit you are all desirable citizens, but the fact remains that our town is called Bunbury." When asked by Dorothy about the ground of the town, he explains, "We dig it out of the ground, which, as you may have observed, is all flour and meal," adding that there is a butter mine on the opposite side of the village. He also converses with another townsman, Mr. Over, asking him directly what he suggests be done.

## Relationships

**[[Dorothy]]** — acquaintance. Their limited exchange over the town's food supply suggests no more than a passing acquaintance.

**[[Billina]]** — enemy. Scant overlap between the two in the record could hint at friction, though nothing in the excerpts confirms this directly.

**[[Pop Over]]** — acquaintance. Appearing together while discussing the town's affairs suggests a working acquaintance among the citizens of Bunbury.

**[[Toto]]** — enemy. The sparse contact between them may indicate tension, though this remains only a suggestion from the available material.

page.title: Rigmarole Town
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Rigmarole Town
- Place type: Village
- Region: Oz
- Status: Defensive Settlement of Oz

## Biography

Rigmarole Town is a village reached by a road that, according to the Wizard, leads there because he enchanted the wagon wheels. Its houses are Munchkin-shaped, and its inhabitants — called Rigmaroles — are so absorbed in their own affairs that they scarcely notice strangers. They are known for answering even simple questions with extremely long, roundabout sentences, as shown when a boy in the town responds to a question about the town's identity with a meandering, unfinished explanation, prompting the Wizard to laugh and remark, "It's a rigmarole because the boy is a Rigmarole and we've come to Rigmarole Town." Alongside Flutterbudget Center, Rigmarole Town is counted among what Omby Amby calls "the Defensive Settlements of Oz."

## Events

The enchanted wagon carrying the Wizard and his companions arrives in Rigmarole Town, a village of Munchkin-shaped houses whose inhabitants speak in extremely long, roundabout sentences.

## References

<references/>

page.title: Lord High Chigglewitz
page.content:
## Biography

Lord High Chigglewitz, aussi connu sous le nom de Larry, est un homme chauve et corpulent. Il porte un habit bleu à boutons de laiton, un gilet rose et une culotte fauve. Il compte parmi les Fuddles, des personnages formés de pièces qu'il faut assembler correctement. Le Cuisinier conseille de commencer par lui pour reconstituer les Fuddles, conseil que le Magicien accueille avec gratitude. Aunt Em découvre la première pièce de son corps, avant que la Poule Jaune, grâce à sa vue perçante, examine les fragments épars et retrouve ceux qui manquent. En moins d'une heure, le vieux Larry se retrouve entièrement reconstitué devant eux.

## Relationships

**[[Aunt Em]]** — acquaintance. Their contact seems tied to the matching of his scattered pieces, during which she is described asking, "Why do you do it?"

**[[Dorothy]]** — acquaintance. Their exchange seems limited to a single moment of gratitude, as old Larry replies, "Thank you, my dear," greatly pleased.

## References

<references/>

status.quote: I will go at once to the kitchen to prepare your dinner.
I will go at once to the kitchen to prepare your dinner.

page.title: Water of Oblivion
page.content:
## Infobox

- Name: Water of Oblivion
- Place type: Fountain
- Region: Land of Oz
- Status: Active

## Biography

The Water of Oblivion is, according to Ozma, "the most dangerous thing in all the Land of Oz." It fills the Forbidden Fountain, and whoever drinks from it at once forgets everything he has ever known. In the past, a King made his people drink of the Water of Oblivion so that they would forget how wicked he had been, and they became as simple and innocent as their King; afterward, they all grew wise together, and their wisdom was good, so that peace and happiness reigned in the land.

## Events

Ozma explains to her companions that the Forbidden Fountain holds the Water of Oblivion, warning that it erases all memory from anyone who drinks it. She and the others then stand on the far side of the fountain to watch what happens, as the ground beyond it gives way and the First and Foremost rises up with his warriors.

## Biography

Judge Sifter is called upon by the King to advise on the fate of a group of captives, taking a position at the King's right hand with the stated duty to "sift this affair to the bottom." When the assembly can offer no further insight, another voice suggests hearing from Judge Sifter, and the King agrees this is proper. Judge Sifter then turns around slowly several times before delivering a verdict: finding nothing against the girl except the stove-hearth upon which she sits, Judge Sifter orders her instantly discharged.

page.title: Blinkem
page.content:
## Biography

Blinkem is an attendant in the King's palace. He informs the King of the time when asked, and announces luncheon, directing a dozen rabbits in livery to bring in trays and arrange the dishes before being dismissed. The King later instructs Bristle to summon Blinkem to attend him immediately, before proceeding to the reception hall.

status.quote: Luncheon is served!" cried Blinkem, throwing open the door, and in came a dozen rabbits in livery, all bearing trays which they placed upon the table, where they arranged the dishes in an orderly manner.

page.title: Pop Over
page.content:
## Biography

Pop Over, also called Mr. Over, welcomes Dorothy alongside Mr. Muffin, offering to feed her when she arrives hungry. He leads Dorothy, Billina, and Toto to his own house, inviting them into his back yard to get waffles. As they walk toward his house, he remarks nervously that he "sort of" hates to let his fence go, suggesting the fence is something he values and is reluctant to part with.

## Biography

The Chief of the Whimsies leads the Whimsies, one of the peoples allied with the Nome King in his campaign against Ozma of Oz. The Chief stood before the Nome King alongside the Grand Gallipoot of the Growleywogs, surrounded by their most skillful generals; so fierce and powerful did the two allied leaders appear that even the Nome King and his General Guph seemed a bit fearful in their presence.

Confident of victory, the Chief of the Whimsies declared, with an evil laugh, that in a few hours Oz would be a desert, echoing the Nome King's own vow that his vengeance upon Ozma of Oz and her people was about to be accomplished.

Later, upon encountering a fountain, the Chief of the Whimsies and his people rushed to drink of its forbidden waters, pushing aside the Growleywogs who had arrived first. In doing so, the Whimsies cast off their false heads in order to drink from the fountain, revealing this practice as part of their nature. The waters both peoples drank were the Water of Oblivion.
